speakeroldname: Rt. Hon. Sir ROBERT BORDEN (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: OFFER OF GIFT FROM THE LORDS AND COMMONS OF THE UNITED KINGDOM.
speechtext:
Some two weeks ago His Honour the Speaker received from the Secretary of the Empire Parliamentary Association in London the following telegram:
London, May 19, 1920.
Rhodes,
Speaker-House Commons,
Ottawa.
Lord Chancellor and Speaker, joint presidents and members of Empire Parliamentary Association in Lords and Commons, ask you to accept as gift to Canadian House Commons the Speaker's Chair as an abiding token of good will between both Parliaments. Suggested that chair should be replica of that in British House of Commons. Colonel Amery, Undersecretary for Colonies, who will be in Ottawa about end of this month, is bringing photographs of British chair and will consult you.
Degvidle,
Commons, London.
Since then Colonel Amery has arrived in Ottawa. He has brought the photograph, which I shall lay upon the table of the House, and which will indicate that the chair which it is intended to send us is beautiful, dignified and ornate. It is my duty now to move a resolution, which I hope my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) will second, setting forth our appreciation of this generous and thoughtful gift and authorizing the Speaker to convey the thanks of this House to the donors. It has been the custom in this House for many years in the past-I do not know how long-that the Speaker upon retiring should take with him as a memorial of his occupancy of the high office of Speaker the chair used during his term. Of course, if this gift is accepted, that custom could not very well prevail in the future.

subtopic: OFFER OF GIFT FROM THE LORDS AND COMMONS OF THE UNITED KINGDOM.
speechtext: Give him a photograph of it.

subtopic: OFFER OF GIFT FROM THE LORDS AND COMMONS OF THE UNITED KINGDOM.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: OFFER OF GIFT FROM THE LORDS AND COMMONS OF THE UNITED KINGDOM.
speechtext: My right hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce suggests that a photograph of the chair might be presented to the Speaker in lieu of the chair itself.

subtopic: OFFER OF GIFT FROM THE LORDS AND COMMONS OF THE UNITED KINGDOM.
speechtext: Give him a gold miniature.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: OFFER OF GIFT FROM THE LORDS AND COMMONS OF THE UNITED KINGDOM.
speechtext:
What may be done in the circumstances would be for hon. members to decide. It may be the pleasure of the House that some memorial, possibly a chair such as has been in the past used by the Speaker, be presented to each Speaker upon his retirement. But that question does not arise at the moment.
It only remains for me to say that since the Parliament House which stood upon this site was destroyed by tire a few years ago we have already been favoured with many indications of the good-will of our brethren in the great Mother Parliament beyond the seas. This further token of good-will is but another illustration of the spirit of comradeship which prevails between the members of this Parliament and the members of the old Parliament in the United Kingdom. We are united by the ties of common ideals, of like institutions and traditions, and of a common allegiance. I hope that it may be our purpose now and at all times in the future to work with them in the best of good feeling and co-operation for the fulfilment of the aims of advanced democracy.

subtopic: OFFER OF GIFT FROM THE LORDS AND COMMONS OF THE UNITED KINGDOM.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: OFFER OF GIFT FROM THE LORDS AND COMMONS OF THE UNITED KINGDOM.
speechtext:
I hope that the House will accept the resolution which I now propose, and which will be seconded by Mr. Mackenzie King:
That the offer of a Speaker's Chair to the House of Commons of Canada by the Lord Chancellor and the Speaker of the House of Commons as Joint presidents and by the members of the Empire Parliamentary Association in the House of Lords and in the House of Commons of the United Kingdom be most gratefully accepted, and that Mr. Speaker do inform the donors of the high appreciation of this House for the gift and particularly for the sympathy and good-will which it expresses.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: OFFER OF GIFT FROM THE LORDS AND COMMONS OF THE UNITED KINGDOM.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of hon. gentlemen on this side of the House it affords me great pleasure to have the opportunity of seconding the motion which has been made in such appropriate words 2051
by my right hon. friend (Sir Robert Borden). If there is one thing above another which we in Canada have reason to be proud of and to be grateful for, it is that our constitution and parliamentary institutions are to all intents and purposes a replica of the constitution and parliamentary institutions of the Mother of Parliaments in the Old World. A visible sign of this great invisible reality such as is embodied in the gift it is our privilege to accept, is one of the links of Empire which make for that unity we all desire in the things which are fundamental to liberty and to the preservation of it.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Motion agreed to.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

maintopic: MEN RELEASED ON HABEAS CORPUS RE-ARRESTED.
speechtext: [DOT] I notice in the press a report that two young men from somewhere near Sherbrooke in Quebec applied recently for a writ of habeas corpus. They had been sentenced to twenty-five years' imprisonment by Mr. Justice Desy of Three Rivers, who happened to sit as a judge of criminal jurisdiction at Sherbrooke. The two young men made application through their counsel, Mr. Cabana, K.C., for a writ of habeas corpus before Mr. Justice Duelos, and the writ was issued by him. I notice in yesterday's press that by order of the Department of Justice at Ottawa the two young men were re-arrested Saturday. Would the Minister of Justice kindly inform the House if the facts as stated are true, and if so, the reasons why the writ of habeas corpus has thus been ignored. This is a very serious matter.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) :
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: MEN RELEASED ON HABEAS CORPUS RE-ARRESTED.
speechtext: As to the facts as stated by the hon. gentleman, I was not aware that these young men had been re-arrested.

maintopic: MEN RELEASED ON HABEAS CORPUS RE-ARRESTED.
speechtext: I read it in the newspapers.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: MEN RELEASED ON HABEAS CORPUS RE-ARRESTED.
speechtext:
I will inquire as to
that. It is a fact that two (men who had been found guilty of a very grave crime, and who had been sentenced to a long period in the penitentiary, were some little time ago ordered to be released upon a writ of habeas corpus by a judge of the Superior Couit in the province of Quebec. Of the proceedings looking to that writ we had no notice, but I presume the Attorney General of the province was heard upon the application. The application was granted.
The matter came to our attention and it was looked into. We were advised that a judge of the Superior Court sitting on a writ of habeas corpus was without jurisdiction to order the release of prisoners duly convictr ed by a court and duly sentenced by a court of at least equal jurisdiction. When the matter was last brought to my attention the question was then under the consideration as to what steps, if any, it was open for us to take for the purpose of having that question passed upon and determined. As I. said, I was not aware that action had actually been taken, but I shall make inquiry and be in a position later to answer fully as to what has been done.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
On.motion of Sir Henry Drayton (Minister of Finance) Bill No. 157 to amend the Business Profits War Tax Act, 1916, was read the second time and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Steele in the Chair.
On section 1-amount of tax charged.

maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
Do the words
"capital employed" in subsection (2) mean the original capital invested?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
There is no
change in the main provisions of the Act relating to capital employed. The change has reference to the rate, so that the tax, so far as the question of capital is concerned, will be levied exactly as it has been in the past,

maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Has the tax been levied on the original capital invested?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext: The actual cash capital invested. This question is covered under section 7 of the main Act which provides that the capital employed in a business or ian incorporated company shall be the amount paid up upon its capital stock.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 2-operation of Act extended for another year.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext: What is the . change here?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext: The effect of the whole section is to extend the time for the operation of the business profits tax twelve months.

maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
I wish to emphasize the point I raised the other day in regard to the exemption from taxation of companies ninety per cent of whose capital is owned by a municipality or a province. This provision undoubtedly constitutes a discrimination, and notwithstanding .anything which my hon. friend may say to the contrary, its effect will be that the operations of one particular business in my own province will bring to the treasury of the country over three-quarters of a million dollars
per year, while the same business in Ontario will not contribute .a single cent to the public. I say that taxation should be the same in all parts of the country, and there is no reason why corporations or companies, a portion of whose capital is owned by a province or a municipality, should be exempt. When a province oir a .municipality enters business it should be treated in precisely the same way as an individual or a private corporation is treated. The minister says that the reason why these corporations in regard to which I complain are exempt is that they will not make any profits. Well, if that is so why put .an exemption clause in the Bill? There is a clause which exempts them frhm paying when their profit does nolt exceed a certain sum. My hon. friend says that they will not have any profit because they are not conducted for the purpose of making profits. Then why do you put an exemption in the Bill? On the other hand, privately owned companies are forbidden by a section of the original law to decrease their rates, as was suggested by an hon. member the other day. Those companies cannot decrease their rates without the leave of the minister; if the minister finds that the price they are charging is too low they can be prevented from decreasing their rates. I do not see why there should be a difference between privately owned companies and publiq concerns.

maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I would like to say something in regard to that particular point and in regard to the operations of the organizations to which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lapointe) has directed attention. Our organizations in Ontario are based on the idea of public service and not profit and if they have profits they distribute them amongst those who are associated with them. If the Hydro-Electric Commission of Ontario makes any profits it distributes them amongst, the municipalities toy means of a reduction in the rates charged for electricity. Because of that, there are practically no profits. They do not desire to 'build up profits tout they do seek to give a public service at cost price and if that is the cage why should they be taxed or interfered with under legislation of this kind?

maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
I have nothing to eay in answer to my hon. friend from South York (Mr. Maclean), except that if the HydroElectric Commission is what he says it is, to the extent that they call it a company instead of -a commission, I am inclined to be-

Have that that organization in Ontario would be practically a private concern. The Government of Ontario had a right to give away whatever powers they deemed it advisable to give to a particular corporation. If it is no longer the province of Ontario that is distributing electrical poweT, I see no reason why this company should not be taxed the same as any other company doing business in a similar way. The province of Quebec has also a good many companies distributing power and electrical energy. The people w'ho have unvested their money in such projects paid taxes to the Government at the rate of $740,000 last year, while in Ontario, just because the Government has created a special corporation, depending to a certain extent on the province, that company will not pay a cent into the federal exchequer. That is unfair competition. If the Government of Ontario hais seen fit to create a special corporation, that corporation should he a corporation like any other and be liable to pay taxes the same as any other. The answer to that contention is that such a corporation is not looking for profit. That is no reason in my opinion because if you take the profits and invest them in your own business again-* which private corporations are prevented from being done by law-there is no reason why a corporation like that in Ontario, having a right to do that, should Ibe exempted from taxes. The fact that in Ontario this corporation have a right to put their money back into the improvement of their property is no reason why they should be exempted from taxation. Take the capital they have put into the proposition, take whatever profit they have made since and 'then find how much they should pay into the public exchequer the same as any other private citizen or corporation.

maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext: The municipalities of Ontario and other portions of the Dominion have the right to use their money and their organization for the distribution, say, of water. They never seek to acquire profit in that manner. They do a large business in that way, and they have a large income. If a city owns its own water system it gives a public service but the money turn over is not profit and such an organization is not called upon to pay taxes on profits.

maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext: If they are not going to make any profit, what is the use of exempting them from the Excess Profits Tax? If they are making mo profit they will have no Excess profits 'tax to pay.

maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext: But the hon. gentleman is trying to make them pay whether they have any profit or not.

maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext: No, hut I do not want them to be treated in a manner different from any other corporation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I do not know that I can usefully add very much to what I have already said on this subject. Rightly or wrongly, certain municipal and governmental activities -are looked upon as being in a different position from the activities of a private corporation, one set of activities -being carried on for gain on the one hand and the other for -service. This question ;is not -merely one between what is perhaps the largest example of that doctrine in the concrete, the Ontario HydroElectric system and private owned companies, but it is a question between private owned companies and a very great number of our municipalities throughout the whole country. Winnipeg ifor example^ has a very excellent electrical plant, it has a large turn over in connection with the supply of electrical power, it is carrying -its investment and carrying it properly out o'f its rates and it is providing for a 'sinking fund. It is carried along exactly in the same wiay as the Hydro-Electric Power Commission of Ontario. I do not know that 'it is -really necessary that -the -exemption should be put in but now that the question is .raised, it- certainly, I think, ought to stand.

maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Why?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Because I have never heard of legislation in a province taxing by right of the province the property of His Majesty as represented by the Dominion; nor have I ever heard of legislation by His -Majesty as represented 'by the Dominion taxing the property of His Majesty as represented by the province.

maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman not realize that the minute -the Government of Ontario, or any other government, parts with i'ts rights by handing them over to a private corporation, his argument falls to- the ground?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
I would entirely agree with my hon. friend if that were the ease. But that is not the case. By no stretch of imagination could a municipality be regarded as -a private corporation or could the Hydro-Electric Power -.Commission he referred to a-s a private company.

It has absolutely none of the adjuncts of a private company.

maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Could action be taken against the corporation itself?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext: No action could be taken against the Hydro-Eledtnc Power Commission except on a flat because it is recognized that it is part of the machinery of the Government of Ontario: It is not in the same position as a company. It has never been found feasible for the Crown as represented by the Dominion to tax the Crown as represented by a province or vice versa. That is a fundamental principle which I am sure will commend itself to every hon. gentleman. It is well 'that it should be made clear at once that .concerns which are not incorporated for the purpose of profit, or concerns set on foot by reason of the action of municipalities or provinces, not for the purpose of making profits, need not do any .accounting under this system. There would foe no use in doing it if they never could have profits. They ought not 'to make profits. If they make profits it is against the whole policy which is to give the cheapest land best service after providing for a sinking fund. It can hardly be said that there is any real discrimination between a company on the one hand earning dividends in excess of ten per cent, and a municipality or a government, or a governmental commission that earns no dividends at all. the matter I think, as I said before, is entirely in the hands of these people. With much deference to the representations made by the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) I am still of the view that companies need not earn excessive profits unless they want to, and they are not taxed unless they do earn excessive profits. I know of no provision of the Act which prevents them from reducing rates. Perhaps my hon. friend could refer me to the section.

maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Yes, subsection 6 of sec tion 6 of. the original Act, 1916.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
But that does
not do it. Perhaps I had better read the section:
Where an incorporated company conducts its business, whether under agreement or otherwise, in such manner as either directly or indirectly to benefit its shareholders or any of them or any person directly or indirectly interested in such company by selling its product or the goods and commodities in which it deals at less than the fair price which might he obtained therefor, the minister may for the purposes of this Act determine the amount which shall be deemed to be the profits of such company for any accounting period, and in
determining such amount the minister shall have regard to the fair price which, but for any agreement, arrangement or understanding might be or could have been obtained for such product, goods and commodities-
There is nothing in the world to say that these people, in the carrying on of their business, cannot reduce their costs to what the Act itself looks upon as a fair price- namely a price which will result in a gain which cannot be called excessive, a gain which will not exceed ten per cent.

maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
Is the Hydro-Electric
Commission of Ontario-my hon. friend of course will know-declared by the legislation concerning it to be a body corporate or is it not?

maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext: That is the point.

maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
I am not considering
the question of whether or not it earns dividends or profits. If it is declared to be a corporation,' with all the .powers, privileges and responsibilities of a corporation, I think it should be taxed, If it is not a corporation, if it can only be assailed by fiat as the Minister of Finance says, I think it changes the situation. If the Hydro-Electric Commission is a body corporate it is going to stand in the same position as the Canadian National Railways Company, and in the latter case, although the Canadian National Railways Company is owned by the Government, assurances have been given to municipalities, that when the Government takes possession of the Grand Trunk, under the arrangement recently made, the right of taxation by the municipalities will remain. In that case they are going to treat the Canadian National Railways, with the consent of the Government, as a private corporation, or if you like it, a public corporation. Whether it earns dividends or profits or not does not touch the point, it seems to me; the whole thing turns on the name. What is in a name? Sometimes a good deal. If this commission is declared by the legislation of Ontario to be a corporate body politic I think it should be taxed..

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
The Hydro-
Electric Commission is merely a governmental commission charged with a trust in favour of the municipalities.

maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext: And the Canadian National Railways Company is charged with a trust by the Dominion Government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
I submit, with all due deference, that at any rate that is not the way in which the directors of ordinary companies regard themselves, whether

they be a railway or anything else. I have an idea that they are looking towards the fruits of an investment in which they are particularly interested, and that is something they never allow to escape their attention. In connection with the HydroElectric Power Commission, the real question, after all, is whose property is it. The property certainly does not belong to that commission but belongs to the Government and will become the property of the municipalities when they have paid the whole amount of the moneys which were necessary in order to create the property. The property is the property of His Majesty in the right of the province.

maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext: If the question is only one as to whom -the property belongs, I must again use the illustration of the Canadian National Railways. The Grand Trunk railway is now virtually the property of the Crown but inasmuch as the Government have declared by legislation <that it belongs to the Canadian National Railways Company, a corporation, the cities and towns of Canada are going to tax the railway property. So I think myself the minister cannot get back to the general question of whose property this is, because if he takes that view he will not allow any city or town m Canada to tax the Grand Trunk.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext: With all due deference, taxation is a matter of strict legal enactment. Ownership also is something which is determined by strict legal enactment, or contract, as the case may be. Now while it is true that the Crown may only own a share of stock in an incorporated company it is true that the company, so long as it is continued as an existing entity -owning and administering the property- may be taxed; and in the same way the principle is not offended when the Crown, instead of owning one share in a company, owns all the shares; the operations are still carried on as in right of the company. Ownership is owned by that company, and the Government are merely owners of the stock. I admit it is a technical distinction but most distinctions are technical.

maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext: This is a restriction.

maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I repeat my question: Is or is not the Ontario Hydro-Electric Power Commission a body corporate?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext: That commission is specifically declared to be a body corporate-

maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext: -for the purpose of carrying out the trust set out in the document. I know of nothing which vests the property in them. I know of nothing -which places them in the same position as a company which would give them the right to set up a claim to the property.

maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
There is a special provision in the Hydro-Electric Power Commission Act of 1917 which exempts that body from taxation. Section 12 (a) says:
Notwithstanding- anything in the Assessment Act contained, land owned by and vested in the Commission shall be subject to assessment at the actual value thereof according to the average value of the land in the locality.
Here the commission are taxed for municipal purposes. The Act goes on to say:
(2) Subsection 1 shall not apply to or include buildings, machinery, works, structures, substructures, superstructures, rails, ties, poles and other property works or improvements owned, used or controlled by the commission, nor an easement in land not owned by the Commission, but all suoh buildings, machinery, works, structures, substructures, superstructures, rails, ties, poles and other property, works or improvements, owned, used or controlled by the Commission, and every such easement or right, shall continue to be exempt from assessment and taxation as heretofore.
It would appear that the land surrounding the line that-they use for transmission purposes is taxed municipally; and if the municipality has the right to tax the commission why would not the Federal Government have the right to do the same thing?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
I would have thought that there is a clear distinction. My hon. friend will see, in the first instance, this body politic has absolutely no moneys of its own whatever. It gets all its moneys-here I speak subject to correction, I have not read the statute over for a long time

from the Ontario Government. Those moneys are voted to it, or else they are moneys which are raised by bonds of the municipalities with the assent of the Government, the proceeds of which go -to this commission, but of ownership, similar to the ownership of the company it has none. Its sole ownership therefore-if you like to call it ownership-is	subject to the
trust of the province, or the trust of the municipality. Now it is perfectly true that in so far as local lands which are in the possession of this commission are now taxable they were not there made specially taxable on the same theory that lands belonging to the Canadian National Railways are made taxable in the different municipalities through which they pass.

It would be unfair to these municipalities if they should get nothing out of it. For years they did get nothing out of it; they are now allowed to get something out of it. The province can make any law it likes imposing charges upon its property for the benefit of the municipality; w.e can make any law we like charging our property for the benefit of the municipality. We did so this year in connection with Ottawa. But that is a very different thing from the proposal that because a province thought fit to tax its property for the purpose of helping some of its other institutions, we for our purposes can tax provincial property.

maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
The Legislature has the
power that my hon. friend has mentioned. It also has the power to make itself a body corporate. When it does that it comes under the general rules applicable to all corporations. They may legislate that they will pay certain taxes on certain things, and having done so they are not exempted under the General Assessment Act of Ontario, section 12A of which provides that land owned by the company shall be assessed at its actual value, taking into consideration the value of surrounding property. Now, the Legislature of Ontario has chosen, having the power to do so, to abandon its rights as a legislature in respect to certain matters and to hand over those rights and powers to a company. If they want to finance that company or to endorse its notes, that is a different thing. If the company cannot pay its obligations the Provincial Government has to come to its rescue. But that does not do away with the fact that this commission comes under the company law of Ontario to all intents and purposes, except as regards the restrictions imposed in the statute creating the commission.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
I should have
thought it was quite clear that this commission could not possibly come within the provisions of the Joint Stock Companies' Act of Ontario. I do not think that a company which is without capital would be recognized as such by any of our companies Acts. Here there is absolutely no capital, absolutely no issue of stock.

maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
We are not discussing
the Hydro-Electric of Ontario exclusively. 'My hon. friend says that there is no issue of stock in that instance. Well, section 5 of the Business Profits War Tax Act exempts the business of any company, commission or association not less than ninety per cent of the stock or capital of which is owned by a province or a municipality. So
there is certainly some stock there, because it is stated to be owned by a municipality or a province. Now, my hon. friend says that the fact that a portion of the stock is owned by the Crown or by the province should prevent us from taxing.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Oh no, it does not unless we say so.

maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
Why should the Bill
establish an exemption where ninety per cent of the stock or capital is owned by a province or municipality? If only eighty-five per cent of the stock is so owned, the tax provided for by this legislation cannot be applied. Surely my hon. friend will admit that when a company is specially incorporated for the purpose of carrying on a particular trade, whatever be the proportion of the stock owned by a province or municipality, that company is still an incorporated body absolutely independent from and different from the province or the Crown.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I agree.

maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
As to the other argument of my hon. friend that this does not constitute any discrimination, I wish to point out that section 6 of the Act provides as follows:
No deductions from the gross profits for depreciation or for any expenditure of a capital nature for renewals, or for the development of a business, or otherwise in respect of the business, shall be allowed, except such amount as appears to the minister to be reasonable and to be properly attributable to the accounting period, and the minister when determining the profits derived from mining shall make an allowance for the exhaustion of the mines.
As to the other section read by my hon. friend, I fail to interpret it in the same way that he does, The publicly owned company, as stated by my hon. friend from South York (Mr. W. F. Maclean) instead of making profits, reduces the rates or employs the profits in the development of its business, while a privately owned company cannot do that without the approval of the minister. So the consumers are suffering,

and that is the point I emphasize. The consumers of a certain article in one part of the country are deprived of a benefit which consumers of a similar article in another part of the country enjoy. My second point is this: after all, it does not speak very favourably for the publicly owned companies that the federal treasury should get three-quarters of a million dollars out of the carrying on by privately owned companies of a certain trade in the province of Quebec, whereas in Ontario corporations which are carrying on the same

business do not pay one cent to the federal treasury. On its face that is unfair.

maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext: While I am not a lawyer and cannot go into the intricacies of this discussion, I may point out that there is a great movement in favour of public ownership. Public ownership is designed to give service, not to afford profit, the Ontario Hydro-Electric Commission have taken over a number of private companies. Take the case of the Ontario Power Company which, before it was taken over by the Hydro-Electric, would have been liable to pay under this law a contribution in the shape of taxes. The remedy for my hon. friend's friends in Quebec, if there be discrimination, lies in the province of Quebec following the example of the province of Ontario. I make the prediction that within the next ten years the province of Quebec will own its power just as Ontario does, and we intend to acquire more power plants and to develop and administer them for the purpose, not of making a profit but of giving service, and if in giving that service there be any surplus, of devoting that surplus to a reduction of rates. Each section of the community that undertakes to consecrate its capital and efforts towards giving a public service at cost, is justified in doing that, and it ought to be encouraged. That is largely the direction in which the world is moving, namely, to turn public services over to the State or to the municipalities.

maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext: And escape taxation.

maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
Perhaps
to escape taxation; but to do something better, to give service at actual cost, to eliminate profits. The hon. gentleman wants to change that tendency which has manifested itself in Ontario in a number of municipalities and which it is perfectly right for those municipalities to follow. If somebody be hurt in the matter or if there be any discrimination, the fault does not lie against those municipalities or public organizations that undertake to give this public service. It is open to Quebec to do the same thing.

maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext: We are doing better and we do not want to go back.

maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
You now are trying to lay down a law. If the people, in their organization as a municipality, or as an association of, imunicipalities, as is the case in Ontario, undertake to give this service without profit, in order to reduce the cost and to, give the entire profit to the

people, they should not be subjected to a tax of this kind. If there be a discrimination,- it is not their fault.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
The debate seems to be
drifting into- a question between public ownership and private ownership, and listening to the debate, I think that had the Government carried out the policy enunciated by the predecessor of the present Minister of Finance, there would be no room for such a discussion to-day. My recollection is that in presenting the business profits tax last session, the then Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) gave the House and the -country clearly to understand that the business profits tax would not be renewed this year, but that it would [DOT] be replaced by an income tax. An income tax is absolutely sound; every person pays; but a business profits tax does not work out to the advantage of this -country. Only last week, w-e listened to the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) delivering his Budget Speech, in which he -clearly intimated that activity and production had been lessened during the past year. Why? Because the money that would have been used to extend business and enlarge industries was gathered in by the Government, and there was no incentive for industries to go on and extend their business. That is one reason why to-day the Minister of Finance is compelled to acknowledge to the 'House and to the -country that there has been a lessened activity throughout Canada during the past year. The best *way to avoid this controversy as between public ownership and private ownership is to get back to the promises made by the predecessor of the Minister of Finance and to do away with this business profits tax which is an injury to our industries and to Canada. Capital is very -timid, and I ask the Minister of Finance how many new industries have been established throughout Canada during the past two or three years; how many new industries are being established to-day and how many industries are being extended to meet the ever increasing trade that we boast of?

maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
You must except Three
Rivers.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
There are practically none,
and there is no justification for the argument advanced by our friends from Ontario who -oppose the suggestion of my hon. friend (Mr. Lapointe). If the publicly owned and operated utilities of Ontario are not making profits, there will be nothing

to pay. All we ask is that you put them on the same basis as similar industries in the other provinces. But I go>
further and suggest to the Minister of Finance that at this session he should make a reassuring statement to the people of Canada that he is going to do away with a tax that is preventing the formation of new industries anid the extension of old ones. The sooner that statement is made, the better for Canada, if we intend to continue developing our industries so as to meet the increasing trade that is open to the world.

maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
After the statement made by my hon. friend (Mr. W. F. Maclean) about the advantages of the system that obtains in Ontario and discriminates against the other provinces, I do not want my hon. friend to think that we are specially pleading for Quebec. If, by any process of law, you are going to exempt Ontario from the payment of taxation, somebody else has to make up the amount. Supposing under the capitalization of the Hydro-Eleetrie Commission of Ontario, they would have to pay a tax of half a million dollars, if they are exempted from paying it, that sum has to be found somewhere else. Ii hon. members want to speak about unfairness, there is another thing that is unfair. This commission, posing as a provincial institution, goes outside of its province and induces manufacturers to come in, with what result? I have here the report of the Canada Cement Company for the 31st December, 1919. This is what they say:
As advised in our last Annual Report, we were unable in 1918, to operate your No. 8 plant, situated at Port Colborne, on account of the failure of the power company to supply power. Since March, 1919, The Ontario power Company, which is owned by the HydroElectric Power Commission of Ontario, has resumed the supply of power to this plant, but we regret the power company is not delivering power in accordance with the terms of its contract, and the service given is so poor that the output of your No. 8 mill is only about 60% of normal, and therefore, its operation is not profitable. This matter has been repeatedly taken up with the power company, but, as yet, the service has not been improved. Until the power company improves the service and supplies power in accordance with the terms of its contract, we cannot look forward to the profitable operation of this mill.
If my hon. friend wants some more examples of the great success- the HydroElectric Commission' have had, let me tell him that a Mr. Cousins went to England, where he advocated the -great superiority of the Hydro-Electric system of Ontario. He returned to -Canada and he wanted the power. What answer did he receive? I
have here a clipping from an Ontario paper, The Times, which reads:
A. M. Russell, President of Baldwin's Canadian Steel Corporation, announces that orders have been issued to Iloge-r Miller and Son, who have a million dollar plant construction contract, to cease operations as the result of failure to secure a contract from the Hydro-Electric Commission guaranteeing an adequate supply of power to operate their plant.

maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext: What has this to do witt the matter under discussion?

maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext: This is to show that, from start to finish, the business works a -disadvantage and a hardship on the otheT provinces, and that the law ought to he amended so that these companies should pay a tax on their capitalization, the same as any ordinary company.

maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext: The only subject now before the committee is an excess profits tax. If we are going to fight -out the question of private versus public ownership, let us take a day off an-d do that.

maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext: No, we had better go outside and fight it out. We are talking generally about the tax on corporations. My hon. friend was telling us that Quebec ought to follow the example of Ontario. I say: No; as long as -privately-owned companies can give us as good service and perhaps better than you are getting, because our companies are never short of power, and we get it .at a lower rate than you are paying, why should you want to get the Crown mixed up in this business -in order to foTego taxation? Where is -the Government going to get its revenue if every public utility is going to be put under the control of the State? Supposing the Canadian Pacific were owned by the State, where would their tax of $6,000,000 go to? The Government would not get it, and my friends and -myself and the masses of the people throughout the country would have to make up the amount.

maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Does not the hon. gentleman prove too much when he says that the people of Quebec by reason of reduced rates from private companies get power at less cost-that -is one end-and then get a profit-that is the other end? $100,000, say, for the decreased rate, and $100,000 for excess profits; that makes $200,000. In Ontario it is not the same at all.

maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
You get no end because in Quebec to get a cheap rate and a profit you must have good management and economy. I have nothing to say against the Hydro Electric. They can run their busi-
*52.36

ness as long as I have not got to pay for it, hut the moment they are exempt I have to pay, and I say it is not right. You should not expect the other provinces to pay for the Hydro Electric of Ontario.

maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext: We have lower rates in Montreal than in Toronto.

maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
I am sure the people of Ontario will appreciate the apparent Solicitude shown in their behalf by the hon. member for Quebec East and the hon. member for Three Rivers. Those who recall the initiation of the Hydro Electric Power Commission by the government of Ontario will recall the many arguments that were then advanced similar to those that have been made here this afternoon. It is rather remarkable that while the hon. member for Quebec East and the hon. member for Three Rivers apparently started out with the same objective, the hon. member for Quebec East is considerably in advance of the hon. member for Three Rivers, in that he admits that the consumers are going to reap the advantage in Ontario, while the hon. member for Three Rivers claims they are going to suffer by reason of public ownership. I can hardly reconcile those two views. My hon. friends need not get so worked up; Hydro Electric in Ontario cannot become liable for taxation under the Bill before the House, because there are no pir'oifits to be taxed. Consequently, it is an absolute waste of time to discuss this matter this afternoon. I think the suggestion of the hon. member for Peterborough was a good one. If hon. gentlemen opposite cannot contain themselves hut have to boil over on every occasion where Ontario is in advance of Quebec. I think if we had a day off to discuss where favours are shown we could show that Ontario has contributed very generously towards enterprises in the province oif Quebec. Railways, for instance, experimental farms, and some other things I might mention. The hon. member for Huntingdon pointed out that capital is nervous in this country. Oh, how much we heard about the nervousness of capital eighteen years ago when this scheme was first launched in the province of Ontario. I can tell my hon. friends that the people of Ontario are pretty well satisfied with the Hydro Electric. It is not perfect by any means, but they are endeavouring to carry out the project, and it has proven to be a great asset to this province.
The hon. member for Three Rivers referred to the lack of power for certain companies-the cement company at Port C'ol-

borne, and Roger Miller and Son Company. It is true they are short of power. Why? Because before the Hydro-Electric Commission was organized, private corporations secured control of nearly all the power that was available at Niagara Falls. There was embodied in the contracts which were made by the Government of the day with these private companies a provision that the Government of Ontario could not enter into competition with them in the development of power at Niagara Falls. These companies have been exporting, as they had a right to do, under their contracts, thousands of horse-power to the United States, and the people of Ontario suffer as a result of private ownership in this province. I believe that the Hydro-Electric has been the greatest benefit the province of Ontario has ever experienced, and notwithstanding the arguments that have been advanced by those w'ho are opposed to public ownership of public utilities in this country it is going to continue to be a success, and a much greater success in the future than in the past. By reason of this provision that was inserted in the contracts with private companies the Ontario Government has been forced to develop power at Chippewa Falls and other places at an expenditure of many millions of dollars.
Reference has been made to the municipalities taxing the commission on the land. These lands were expropriated from the municipalities, the municipalities under the British North America Act have power to levy taxes for municipal purposes. The municipalities were originally the owners of these lands and they are simply continuing to assess the properties that have been expropriated. The Government of Ontario are simply furnishing and expending the money and charging it up to the various municipalities concerned in the undertaking, which so far has been mainly transmitting power to municipalities. I cannot see any object in. Continuing this discussion here this afternoon, unless it be, as I believe it is, an attempt by certain hon. gentlemen opposite 'to discredit public ownership in this country. They do not want to give it a fair chance. From the outset public ownership has encountered stiffer opposition possibly than any other development that has ever been attempted in the interests of the people. I admit that HydroElectric is not perfect; nothing is perfect; you cannot expect perfection. If the hon. member 'for Three Rivers and the hon. member for Quebec East, who, I understand, had this matter up at a previous

sitting of the House, are determined to go on and discuss the pros and cons of public ownership in this country, if they are going to encroach on the good nature of the House, because their attitude cannot be considered otherwise-

maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext: You are speaking much longer than I did.

maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext: -we might just as well understand the situation, because it is certainly not the Bill before the House that has been occupying so much of their time.

maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext: You are occupying the time; I am not.

maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext: You started it and have taken your time.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
Is the minister prepared to
make a statement as to the continuation of this tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I endeavoured to make myself pretty plain on this question. The taxation was a war taxation. It was a taxation whose incidence was not capable of being applied without a good deal of unfairness. That has been developed in the debate in committee the other day, and again to-day. The tax was a rough and ready way of getting revenue at a time when rough and ready methods were necessary, and, after all, it did bring into the treasury a large amount of the profits which were unnecessarily large. It is a tax which you cannot drop at the moment, but it ought to be dropped just as soon as possible. If hon. members are helpful in seeing that measure go through that will get the Government lots of revenue, there will be not much danger of the tax being continued.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext: May I suggest to the minister that we on this side will willingly assist him in measures that will tend towards economy instead of the extravagance we have had during the past few years.

maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Might I suggest that the minister drop the idea, for instance, of erecting expensive buildings for the Mounted Police at Ottawa at a cost of $500,000, to keep 225 m~unted policemen in Ottawa just for the purpose of parading our streets. I think there is ample room there for economy.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
The hon. member is
out of order in discussing that question at this stage.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 3-capital in case of merger of companies:	v

maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Will the minister explain this section?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext: It means that in this day of mergers we are endeavouring to . see that companies shall not escape the taxation which ought to be paid by reason of the introduction of water into the capital of merged companies. We are endeavouring to see that the taxation which ought to be paid will not escape exaction by reason of the introduction of water into the capital of the merged companies. In other words, when company A is incorporated into company B, the capital is not increased by that merger beyond the addition of the two capitals.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext: This section refers to two or more incorporated companies merged or consolidated at any time after the first of January, 1916. Does the minister intend this to be retroactive, and will he collect additional taxes from that time?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: BUSINESS PROFITS WAR TAX ACT, 1916. AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
