speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: Sir HENRY DRAYTON (Minister of Finance) moved the second reading of Bill No. 158 to amend the Income War Tax Act, 1917.
Explain.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The present Bill carries into effect the taxation changes as to incomes as proposed by the Budget Speech and as covered by the resolutions that have been passed, with certain minor amendments which I shall refer to as they are reached.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Motion agreed to, Bill read the second time and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Steele in the Chair.
On section 1-dividends.

May I remind my hon. fuend of the remarks made the other day by the ex-Minister of Labour (Mr. Croth-ers) ? The Income Tax Act is practically incomprehensible by reason of its many amendments, and I would suggest to my hon. friend that this is an opportune mo-' ment for him to consolidate the various provisions of the Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Next year, I think, will be the proper time to consolidate them. The Act in England has been amend-

ed from time to tiriie; it is amended' every year. I think we may consolidate the different provisions of our Act next year.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Will the minister explain the effect of this amendment?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In the administration of this tax we have always treated stock dividends as income, exactly as if money were paid in actual cash. Where companies do not pay dividends but issue stock, which is really a bonus, to their shareholders the stock dividend is treated the same as money.' The Finance Department of the United States has always treated stock dividends in the same way, but since they adopted that principle the Supreme Court of the United States has declared it bad law and taxes paid on stock dividends have had to be returned. We have, always treated stock dividends as taxable and we shall continue to do so, but it is considered better, so far as we are concerned, that the matter should be made free from all doubt by the inclusion of the words:
-"dividends" shall include stock dividends.
What will be the basis of taxation on stock which is issued at 100 but which when put on the market is sold at 50?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The justification of the dividend is the distribution of surplus. The question is, how much was that surplus reduced by issue of the dividend? To .the extent that you take money out of surplus account, whether by payment of dividend or through the issuing of stock, you lift it from one column and put it into the other and to that extent you are taxed.

Suppose a company issues to its shareholders stock which is afterwards quoted on the market at 50. Will the shareholder be taxed on the basis of 100, the value of the stock when he received it, or on the basis of the market quotation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The price has nothing to do with it. The question of what is paid outside has nothing to do with it. It is a question of the change in the company's surplus and the percentage by which that particular shareholder benefits by that change.
We are now discussing the income war tax? '

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
Is that applicable to a company or to an individual?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is applicable to a company in so far as it is a direct tax to the extent of ten per cent.

There is undoubtedly a misunderstanding in connection with this matter and we might as well clear it up. We will take the case of a company that has a large surplus. The surplus of that company is not taxable and it may, and invariably is, invested in plant, machinery and stock. If the company pays a stock dividend it reduces that surplus by so/ much and issues stock against it. The company has got its surplus capital invested in additional plant and machinery and it has issued stock against that. That is quite clear; anybody can follow that. In the United States they undertook to tax these stock dividends that had been issued by large corporations. The surplus is taken and re-invested and capital stock is issued against it. That is exactly the procedure that an ordinary individual follows if he increases the capacity of his mill. He takes his surplus earnlings, makes an addition to his factory and puts in more machinery. The United States Government undertook to tax stock dividends. The question was argued before the Supreme Court and the court held that this was surplus of the company and that although stock was issued against it, it was not taxable. That is the condition of affairs in the United States. This Government wants to see whether twe can tax further than they do in the United States. They are not going to leave Canadian companies in the same position as American companies. Of course we want a lot of American companies to come in here and develop our resources and this will be a very great inducement for them to come in. I do not think it is good policy to say that stock dividends are taxable. As a matter of law that was argued in the United States and the Supreme Court decided against that policy. Regardless of what the minister tells the House that is a fact. It is .a question for the House to consider whether we are prepared to go further than the United States have gone. I think the more gracious procedure for this Government to follow would be to accept the American precedent and declare that stock dividends shall not be taxable. I think hon. gentlemen understand the point. The surplus capital is invested in plant and machinery and stock is issued against that capital. That becomes the property of the stock-

holders of the undertaking and it gives them that amount of additional capital.
Mr. DuTREMBLAY:	Do I understand
that depreciation will be taxed by this new clause?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Depreciation
cannot be distributed if it is properly charged.

May I draw the attention of the minister to the construction which may be put on those words "stock dividends"? The minister has given us, very properly, the policy of the department which is to tax the actual money which is taken and distributed but which instead of being distributed to the shareholders goes to the treasury of the company and stock is issued in lieu thereof. That is the policy of the department but the law does not say that. The law does not say that t'he tax is due on the face value of the shares given in dividends or ainy money which is actually taken from the treasury ias liquid assets and put back into another account in the books of the company. There may be a misunderstanding as to the interpretation of the law. The minister has given the department's construction of the law but the law will be submitted to the interpretation of the tribunals and it is possible that they may put upon the terms of the law a different construction and may take the face value of the stock as the amount of dividends distributed instead of the actual amount of money which, instead of being distributed as a cash dividend has been put back under a different heading in the books of the company, shares for that capital investment being issued and distributed in lieu thereof. I think the wording of this provision might be improved.

I would like to .ask how this clause would operate if the dividend shares paid happened to be shares of no par value such as are being issued in the United States very largely and likely in this country also.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not think there will be very much trouble in that regard. What is done is this: You must have a surplus in a properly managed company, in order to enable you to have a stock dividend. The theory of a stock dividend is that a company, having money or assets in its hands which it would not desire to distribute to the shareholders but would require to keep in its own possession, issues in place of that money or cash a stock divi-206
dend. It would miake in practice no difference whether you gave dividends or gave specific shares. The amount that is realized, or that is taxable, is the amount of the surplus which ceases tot be the property of the company as a company and becomes the property of the shareholders as the .result of the issue of that new stock.

I would like to ;ask if these surpluses, to which allusion is made, and against which additional stock is issued, have not .already paid a tax in the form of the special tax on corporations? As I understand, a company pays the corporation tax on its earnings during the year and if it achieves a surplus, that surplus has already paid .a tax in the form Of the corporation tax.
M.r. NESBITT: As I understand it, stock dividends lare treated, when received by individual shareholders as cash dividends, in calculating the income of an individual shareholder?	.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
It therefore increases the issued stock of the corporation.
I would like to hear from the minister whether he proposes to follow the American practice or go them one better.
Do not talk about "trade with the Yankees."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What is proposed is to continue what we have done and to make no difference between the earnings which are distributed as cash dividends on the one hand and the earnings which are distributed as stock dividends on the other. In so far as the American situation is concerned it was obvious, of course, that they would do just exactly what we have been doing and as a matter of fact-although their Supreme 'Court, as I stated in opening, said that the Act was unconstitutional, -legislation, as I am at present advised, is now pending which will get away from the defects of the former Act and allow the tax to be levied.

What I am afraid of, Mr. Chairman, is that if a question should go to the courts the courts may take as a basis of the taxation, not the actual cash which is disposed of by the company but the face value of the stock issued in dividends. There is nothing in the Act which says that the actual basis of the Act shall be the cash



so distributed. The cash is not distributed, I understand-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is all that could be taken, the hon. gentleman will see.

No.
iSdr HENRY DRAYTON: It is only what the company gives up to the shareholder that could be taxed.

No, because you say that the tax shall apply to stock dividends. If you issue stock at the par value cuf twenty-five, for instance, you can tax on the face value of the stock issued, and you are still within the application of the law. There is nothing stated to the effect that it is the cash which is the basis of the dividends distributed which is going to be assessed.
I think that if the minister will say that the stock dividend is supposed to be distributed on the par value that will meet my hon. friend's point.

Rut supposing there is no
par value mentioned? There are in Canada some provinces-the province of Quebec among the number-which authorize the issue by companies of stock with no par value, and there is no par value attributed to the shares. Here again is shown the double interpretation which may be given to this Act. 'Suppose that these shares issued, taken at their par value, are at 40, and that the cash which represents these shares is not of the same amount. Then a double construction will be possible. It will be possible either to tax the shares at their par value, or to tax the money which represents the shares that have been issued. I do not know whether I have made my argument clear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I cannot quite
follow my hon. friend. There is no thought here of taxing stock as stock. We are not taxing stock as stock; all we are doing is to say that a company cannot cheat the revenue by paying stock dividinds instead of cash dividends-that is all we are doing. There is no taxation on a share as a share; that is where my hon. friend mistakes the point. This is merely enlarging the definition of income to say that to the extent that expenditure has been plussed by bringing in in that one year-and only in that one year -stock dividends paid out of profits by the companies that it shall be considered as income; and the amount of that income-just in the same way as the amount oif the cash dividends-must be the amount by 
which the company has depleted its surplus or other cash reserves.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext: While I do not for a moment retreat from the position I took a while ago that nothing should be done to tax business and prevent its expansion, it seems to me that the minister here is on sound ground when he is placing incorporated companies on exactly the same basis as partnerships. It is unfair to partnerships that they should be taxed up to the limit and that incorporated companies should be allowed to escape in respect of stock dividends.

I would like to direct
the attention of the minister to another way of escaping the payment of income tax. I have noticed that of late-to be correct,, ever since this legislation has been in force, -huge advertisements, advertisements of inordinate size have been published in the newspapers, especially in the automobile world. Evidently these companies have been doing an immense business during the war and since, and they are spending on advertisements profits which ought to be taxed by my hon. friend.
They are American companies.
And Canadian companies too. This is a way of evading the payment of taxation, and I call upon my hon. friend the minister to reach these companies.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 2-determination of deficits and losses:
Will the minister explain what is the purpose of this amendment? The amendment itself is there but not the clause which is proposed to be amended.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There are certain deductions which are allowed to be' made from income, and the particular clause which is amended is clause (f) of Section 2 of the Act of 1919. That is to say, supposing a lawyer, making $10,000 a year, goes into some side venture and loses $2,000 he cannot deduct that $2,000 from his regular income.
He cannot?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, he cannot. In order to make it clear so that there can be no doubt as to what is or is not a debt or loss, having regard to that main business, it is proposed to add this section:

-and the minister shall have power to determine what deficits or losses sustained in transactions entered into for profit are connected with the chief business, trade, profession or occupation of the taxpayer, and his decision shall be final and conclusive.
In the previous legislation the principle is laid down. Here the machinery is provided for seeing that the principle is lived up to.

In other words, it means that when a man has two or three lines of business and earns an income from one and loses more than he makes in another, he does not get any reduction on the losses that he suffers. That is exactly what the provision means and I do not think it is fair. Suppose a man is interested in two lines of business; he makes on one and loses on the other. He pays income tax in respect of the business which yields him a profit, but for the loss that he incurs in the carrying on of the other business he gets no allowance.

If a man makes a profit in one business and incurs a loss in another, it is probable that his income will be nil, and if he has no income he should not be taxed. It is immaterial what he makes it out of so long as he pays the tax according to his income.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Take the case
of a man who is interested in three different manufacturing companies. His main business is manufacturing, and he would be taxed on his net income from those three companies.

Suppose a professional man has stock in two lines* of manufacture, making a profit in one and losing in the other. Would he 'be taxed in respect of the business which yielded him a profit, or would the whole thing be taken together?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There, of course, it would be different; that is where the amendment would come in. The question would be whether he was a professional man or a manufacturer. It would seem to me that in the case mentioned he would* be a professional man having stock in these companies. If there was a loss in these companies, of course he would get no dividends, but on the other hand he would not be allowed to charge up against his professional income, income derived from the carrying on of his main business, losses incurred in that venture he took in the manu-facutring business.

I suppose it would depend on what decision was arrived at as to what was his chief business?
206*

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That would* be the point to be determined.

Is it important to draw a distinction between one business and another? It is not a crime for a professional man to put some money into a manufacturing business; I do not see why he should be obliged to declare which is his chief business. Take the case of a medical man who engages in the manufacture of medicine, is he a professional man or a manufacturer? I do not see what difference it makes to the minister how the income is derived. If a man gets the income, he should be taxed; if he does not, I do not see how you are going to tax him.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I agree in large part with my hon. friend. But the real issue is not the question of manufacturing on the one side and professional work on the other. The real issue is this: Once a man actually gets an income from his main occupation or source of revenue he should be taxed, and he should not be allowed to subtract from that main income losses which he runs into in other directions. Let me illustrate. In all our large cities, particularly in Toronto, there are a lot of agriculturists, if I may use the word, as distinguished from farmers. I refer to men who make their money in the city, but who have farms just outside the city in connection with which they lose money. I have known such men to contend that while the income from their profession or from the carrying on of their business was $25,000 a year, it was unfair to tax them on that 'basis because they were losing $10,000 to $15,000 a year in the running of farms a few miles out of the city. It is to prevent that sort of thing that the amendment is introduced. That man really is not a farmer. He has his main net income, and if he chooses to spend it in carrying on this outside activity, he is in the same position as the man who spends it on automobiles or anything of that kind.

These cases cannot be very numerous. I am inclined to think that if a man has made money in his profession and sees fit to carry on farming operations as a hobby, he cannot lose a great deal in that connection without doing some good to the community. If my hon. friend makes a fortune in his capacity as Minister of Finance, which he is pretty certain to do, and wants to invest some of it in a farm,
I am not sure that we should penalize him for doing so. If it is a fad, it is a worthy fad, one which makes for many good things for our country. But the point is this: At

the end of a year you ask a man how much his income was from all sources. If he has not the income, how are you going to make him pay? If he has a professional income of $10,000 and has lost $15,000 in the operation of a farm he is just $5,000 in debt to some one; where is he going to get the money to pay the tax? After all, the rough and ready way of putting it is this: Has a man the income? If he has, let him pay the tax; if he has not, he cannot pay the tax. It is not to he assumed that a man goes into a business on the side merely for amusement; he goes into it for legitimate purposes, and if he loses money, I think it is one of the laws of trade that he should not he penalized for it. But you cannot make a man pay if he has not the money.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Income under our Income Tax Act is not net income; it is income before any charge is made against it, and (the effect of what we are doing here is simply to carry that principle out in its general application, not only to the things that you may choose to do with, perhaps, no particular object in view, but to the things that you have to do or desire to do for a very particular purpose. It is true that the man with an income of $10,000 a year has to maintain a household and supply his family with the necessaries of life, and so on. He has a lot of charges to make against that income; probably he even has no net income. Now, we are saying that these essential expenditures will stand in exactly the same position as an expenditure of the kind that he need not go into; that a loss in .connection with another activity than that from which he derives his main income cannot be deducted from that income any more than can his other unescapable expenditures.

This brings us a little nearer to the question of the taxing of the indemnity of members of the House. I understand that amounts expended in the earning of an income may properly be charged against that income. Let us suppose (that a member of this House has a total income of $2,500 a year, which is the indemnity, and that in order to earn this indemnity he spends $2,000 a year,-all in connection with the fulfilment of his public duties ias a member o'f Parliament. Is not this expenditure properly chargeable against (the total indemnity, just as expenditure ordinarily incurred in the earning of itocome is chargeable against .that income for the purposes of the tax? I wonder if the minister sees the point I am making.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have it exactly, *and as a matter of fairness I entirely agree with my hon. friend.
Then why don't you do it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, I miay do it. In the first instance, I should have thought is ,was very debatable whether members of Parliament should be taxed or not on. 'their indemnity, because it is not supposed to be an income, it is supposed to be an indemnity; but Parliament itself decided that if wanted to be taxed. Apiparenty, members of Parliament, with wonderful unanimity, determined that they would like to be taxed.
Not at all. I may remind the minister that this was a straight declaration made by his predecessor without anybody calling for it.
I asked to be exempted.

I brought this matter up the first time the income tax was introduced, and the minister's predecessor said, just as my hon. friend1 has said, that he thought that, properly speaking, the indemnity should not be taxed. But it was taxed, and at that time I put up a fight with the department that if we were to call this indemnity an income, we should be allowed our necessary expenditures in earning that income. The next year the former Minister of Finance, as the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Beiland) says, deliberately put in the Act a clause that we should pay on the full indemnity without any allowance. As an individual is allowed to deduct, not personal expenses, but office expenses incurred in earning an income, members of Parliament have an equal right to be allowed to deduct expenses incurred in earning what is called our sessional indemnity. I quite agree that if that were done, there would, in many cases, be no income to be taxed.
We would have a claim against the State.

My hon. friend (Mr. Lapointe) says that we would have a claim against the State. But either the indemnity ought to be exempt from taxation or we ought to be allowed to deduct necessary expenses in earning the income. It was only because of the delicacy of the matter on the part of hon. members that it was not opposed at the time. It was a mistake that it was not opposed.

I do not -want to appear before the committee as claiming that that part of the indemnity which is net income should not be taxed, but I claim that whatever expenditure is incurred in connection with the fulfilment of our public duties should toe charged against the total indemnity-
Including election expenses.
-and in that case, I am sure the minister's department would not get very much money out of the members.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman think that contributions for election expenses or anything of that kind should be deducted?
We do not expend anything for that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think the
proper thing would be that a fair per diem allowance, which would represent the expenses of a member while in Ottawa and while the House is in session, should be deducted before the amount is assessed.
Hear, hear. *

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Perhaps that is something which we might regard as a matter of administration. As the Bill is a fairly long one I do not suppose that we shall finish it to-day, and the matter will not be lost sight of.
Could not some means be devised of collecting income tax from people who are not actually resident for twelve months in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That matter is dealt with later on.

Does not the minister think it is too drastic to make the decision of the minister final and conclusive? If ahy difficulty arises between the department and1 the ratepayer, the matter should be submitted to the Exchequer Court of Canada, which is a court provided expressly for the purpose of arbitrating between the Crown and its subjects.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 4-income from an estate or accumulating in trust:

If a man is a beneficiary and certain moneys accrue in a certain year and they are not paid in that year, why should they be taxable in that year? Supposing I am an executor for an estate, and certain moneys that should be paid into the estate during a certain calendar year, are not paid in during that year but are paid in the next year, if they are taxable in the previous year, a mix-up will occur in the accounting of the estate.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is thought- and this is the result of the experience of the department-that it is a great deal better for accretions to be taxed regularly; that you should not have delayed taxes, because when taxes are delayed, too much must be paid all at once. It is really in the interest of the beneficiary himself, that when he cannot draw his income, the proper charges against that income which, after all, is actually earned-and what we should get is a tax on money when earned, whether distributed or not-should be paid.
He might not get the money at all. Very frequently we do not get money that properly should be paid into an estate.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In that case, the tax would not have to toe paid. That would not toe income, because it would not be received.
The clause reads that if the income accrues in that term, the tax must be paid. Such an exaction is an injustice.

I should like to refer to the returns made by members of Parliament. Many members of Parliament who are in business take stock each year on the 31st of January or some time during that month. They are expected by the department, I understand, to include their sessional indemnity in the return for the accounting period. For instance; if the accounting period for the year- 1920 is arrived at in the month of January of that year, the department has ruled that the return must include the indemnity for 1920, before it has toeen received. (Suppose a member of Parliament sends in his return in January and includes in it the indemnity he expects to receive during the year, and that in the meantime a general election comes and he does not receive the indemnity, he will have to pay taxes on an indemnity he has not received. I think in a case of that kind the member should include only hils returns for the accounting period ending on the 31st of January or on the date mentioned in the schedule.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I should like
this section to stand.
Section stands.
On section 5-Patriotic and Red Cross funds:

I wish to suggest to the
committee that instead of repealing paragraph (c) it should he amended in such a manner as to allow the exemption of amounts paid by the taxpayer during the year for charitable purposes. Paragraph (c) reads as follows:
-amounts paid by the taxpayer during the year to the Patriotic and Canadian Red Cross funds, and other patriotic and war funds approved by the minister;
It is quite clear that war funds are no longer in existence, so they should not be considered. It is quite true that the Patriotic fund is still in existence, and gifts might still be made to it. The Red Cross fund is also in existence, as it has been for many years. My suggestion would be that the paragraph should be allowed to stand and that in place of the word " war " the word " charitable " should be inserted, so that amounts paid to any of the above named funds and to charitable funds during the year will be exempted. The Act by paragraph (d) of section 5 now exempts the income of charitable .institutions, hut it does not exempt gifts to such institutions when made by the ordinary taxpayer. In the province of Ontario, where there is an ever increasing succession duty payable on death, the Act has always exempted from the tax legacies for charitable, religious and educational purposes. Nor do I think there has been any great loss to the province or any harm done by reason of that law. The American Act specially exempts such gifts up to the amount of 15 per cent of the taxpayer's entire income. Their clause is much wider than the one I have suggested, it reads:
Contributions or gifts made within the taxable year to corporations organized and operated exclusively for religious, charitable, scientific, or educational purposes,
And so on.
to an amount not in excess of 15 per cent of the taxpayer's net income.
I think this is a matter which might receive the favourable consideration of the committee. We all know that these charitable institutions must be kept up, and are largely kept up, by voluntary contributions, and that most of these contributions come from a limited number of people in
[Mr. Pedlow.l
each locality. It is not altogether the wealthy man who supports these charities. It is the man of moderate income, who is called upon time and again throughout the year, and who wishes to, and who does subscribe to the fullest extent for the maintenance of these institutions. It is a little hard and I think ungenerous for this country, after that subscription has toeen made, to force the giver -to pay an income tax thereon. I do not know that one can elaborate or add anything to this plea. I would suggest the following amendment moved by myself and seconded by the hon. member for North Perth:
That paragraph (c) of subsection 1 of section 3 be amended by substituting the word "charitable" in the place of the word "war" in the last line of the said paragraph.

Does my hon. friend
move that as a substitute for section 5?
Yes.
My hon. friend is referring to the Act as it now stands, and not to the Bill, and he may have to change his amendment slightly.
Yes. Unfortunately, having just come down from a committee meeting, I had not seen the Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The section
which the hon. member desires to amend is paragraph (c) of subsection 1 of section 3 of the Act- of 1917, which reads as follows:
(c) amounts paid by the taxpayer during the year to the Patriotic and Canadian Red Cross funds, and other patriotic and war funds approved by the minister.
I understand that- he desires to substitute the word " charitable " for the word " war." I suppose that everybody likes to encourage charity, but after all charity sometimes begins at home. We have a very heavy task in raising the necessary revenue. I do not know just exactly how much the charitable people of this country, and there are many of them, would have their hands stayed by the fact that they had to pay their share towards the country's expenses, or how much more or how much less would be given in consequence of our action in this matter. I do not like, so far as I am concerned, to say no directly to my hon. friend's suggestion. It is a subject which deserves consideration. I would at any rate suggest to my hon. friend that he limit the exemption as provided by the American legislation, which limits it to an amount not in excess of 15 per cent of the taxable income. That is, the American Government says:

If you want to do your duty as you see it, and look after charitable objects to the extent of 15 per cent of your taxes we will help you to do it. The charity is at the expense of the Government to the extent of 15 per cent only. I would suggest that if we substitute Government aid for the generous and spontaneous action of charitable persons we ought t'o have at least some limitation, as exists in America, to the extent that that aid should be given.
Say 10 per cent.

Much as I sympathize with the hon. member for London (Mr. Cronyn) and the hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. Currie) in their desire Ito encourage charitable grants, it seems to me that there are two great objections to 'the motion of the hon. member for London, and the first objection is given by the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton), who -says that this is ta charity at the expense of the State. The first -duty of every citizen is towards the State, land no money of (Which the country stands so much in need should be diverted from the aid of the State to charitable institutions, which undoubtedly are deserving of every consideration hut which must be subordinated to the interests of itlhe 'country. Charitable institutions are deserving, it is true, but there is no institution which should appeal more to the consideration of the -citizen than the State. The second objection I have to the motion is the difficulty which it creates for the Minister of Finance in determining what are charitable institutions and charitable objects. There -are a thousand and one charitable funds and institutions throughout Canada, and we are to give to the Minister of Finance the discretion to determine which of them will, and which will not, be favoured. Grants to some of them will be deducted from income and grants to others will nolt, and I think that if the motion is adopted (the position of 'the Minister of Finance will be made very difficult indeed. Broad minded and fair minded as he is, we can -readily understand that his position would be an invidious one under such circumstances, and I therefore think that it iwlill Ibe best to* stand by 'the general law. As the minister has pointed out, I do not think any one will be hindered from making grants to' 'Charitable Institutions whi'dh deserve assistance from wealthy people.

It might toe inferred from the hon. gentleman's lucid remarks

that he desires charity to contribute to the waT. The Sick Children's Hospital will pay this tax; the sick children will 'be the payers.
Does the hon. gentleman think that the determination not to deduct grants from the income will deter rich people from making such grants?
I do not know that it will; I am not prepared to say so. But I understand thlait this will be deducted from the amount given to charity.
No>, from the income.
It is the same thing.
No.
Is there no loss to charity under this?
Not at all.
What is the hon. gentleman's argument?

The argument is that under the motion of the hon. member for London a man who has an income taxable will have the right to deduct from that income whatever grants he makes to charitable institutions. If we accept that motion it will not be the tebaritable institution that will be called upon to pay the tax; the man that makes the grant will have the right to deduct from his taxable income whatever he has given ,as a grant, and therefore I say that it will not prevent a rich man from making a grant to charitable institutions.

It certainly will deter a man from making such a grant. It is to be supposed that in making the grant be is giving as large an amount as he can, .and therefore if he has to pay the tax it will reduce the grant by that much. In this case, (therefore, the loss will be that 01E the sick children, and in the final analysis they pay the tax.

In the example given by the hon. member (Mr. Currie) which prompted my hon. friend to rise,-I refer to the charity loft to the sick .children-i't is not the grant itself that will he taxed but the balance of the estate.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
I think the members of the House would favour the amendment made by the hon. member for London (M(r. Cronyn) providing they were perfectly sure of the construction that would he given to the words "other charities." In the section amended, which he mentioned are the
(Mr. Burnham.]
Patriotic Fund, the Red Cross and other charities. If "other charities" means, applying the rule of law, ejusdem generis, of a like nature, I am quite willing to have the amendment passed but if it is going to be construed in such a way that it may include religious institutions of all kinds or institutions that deal with other matters than bodily infirmities and the like I am inclined to think that it would be very ill-advised to make such an exemption because it would place on the shoulders of the Minister of Finance the delicate responsibility of deciding which should be regarded as a charity. We might have contributions to churches that would be claimed as being exempt from income tax. I think it would be well that it should be construed as the Patriotic Fund, Red Cross, and other charities of a similar nature. I should like to hear the view of the. minister as to what charities along these lines should be exempt.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext:
Reading this clause in the
Bill, it occurs to me that there must have been some truth in the statement published in the daily press during the years of the war that certain parties in Canada had subscribed generously to the Patriotic and Red Cross funds, but had never paid and the consequence was they were enabled to escape the assessment made by the Department of Finance. I have it in my mind now that the minister is going to guard against that in this Bill.

It appears to me that the object of this committee is to find means of getting revenue to run the country. Instead of making loop-holes to lose revenue we should rather tighten up the provisions of the income tax law so that this country will have sufficient money to pay its debts. It appears to me that the amendment as submitted is a dangerous one. What limit's would you put on it? It opens the way to all kinds of false declarations and it puts the minister in the awkward position that he has to take the responsibility of depiding what should be exempt and what should not be exempt from taxation. I would rather see the minister go a little bit further and wipe out every exception. A man who gives charity gets enough credit for it without wanting to have his contribution exempted from taxation. Every man should be willing to pay his just share of taxes towards running the business of the country and I am not in sympathy with making loop-holes to let any man evade his fair share of taxes. I would rather tighten

up, make it as equal as we can and make every person in the country large or small, bear his proportionate share of the expenses of the country. It should be put on a business basis and I am glad the Minister of Finance is trying here to make us pay our way the same as any business man, or honest man would pay his way and to enable us to run this country on a business basis.
Shall the amendment, be adopted?

I would like to suggest
that the paragraph stand to let the minister have an opportunity of looking it over. I am quite sympathetic with any real charity. It- looks as if it might be quite feasible for some things to be brought under the head of charity that really are not charity. I am quite in accord with the proposal that the word " charity " shall be added. I have not a memorandum here of the original clause. The Bill just says that a certain clause shall be struck out. I would like to suggest that the word " patriotic " be dropped. That does not apply very frequently now. What would you call a patriotic association? When the war was on there were certain things that could easily be described by the word " patriotic " but these organizations are unnecessary now. I do not think it would be hard to define what " charities " are. That is why I suggest the minister allow the paragraph to stand, give it some thought and see if the word " charities " could not be so defined that it would include only what the hon. member for London has in his mind; that is a real, actual charity. I do not agree with the statement that a man who generally gives to charity is a man who is getting any advertisement out of it. A man who generally gives to charity gives for charity's sake and gets no benefit or advertising. I assume that he gives it secretly and that he gives it out of the goodness of his heart.

I quite agree with my hon. friend from Lotbiniere (Mr. Vien) that this provision would not prevent a rich man from giving to charity if he wished to do so. There are many rich men-and we all rejoice that it is so-whose hearts are as big as their, fortunes, and I have no doubt that they would still give. But what the hon. member for London states is true that after all, the multitude of those who contribute towards charity are not rich men. They are mostly men of very moderate means and it is that class of contributor who would benefit by the amendment proposed by the
hon. member for London. The man who has a fortune and gives a few thousand dollars does not miss that amount, but the man of very moderate income who receives every week of his life some application for a contribution to a worthy charity, in the aggregate gives quite a percentage of his ordinary income in that way. If he could be exempted from the payment of taxes on those contributions it would rather encourage him to give. I am sorry for the Minister of Finance, who is going to be in a very difficult position if he has to determine what is a charity and what is not. But he has lots of difficulties these days and adding one more to his troubles is only a small matter. There is much to be said on both sides, but I think that the weight of the argument falls on the side of the hon. member for London.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: How would the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fielding) propose to check the payments made for charitable purposes? How could you have the word " charity " in the Act and not give it an elastic meaning. Suppose it had an elastic meaning? There are very few churches that do not carry on a good deal of charitable work. How would you find out what was given for charitable work in connection with a church? One man might go to church and put $5 on the plate and not advertise the fact while another man might. I see great difficulty in ascertaining what is the meaning of the word " charity " unless you tie it down to certain organizations. By leaving it general and wide open I doubt if we would ever get anywhere.

Do I understand the
minister to say that the amendment as it stands in the Bill does away with these exceptions?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

I entirely agree with
that-. I do no,t think there should be any cheese-paring at all. I think it better to strike them out altogether.

There is still another
objection to extending the exemption to contributions to charitable institutions, although it may not be a very formidable one. The objects mentioned in the Act of 1917 were of a national character and one making a contribution to the Patriotic Fund was making a contribution to a fund for all Canada. If you alter that and exempt the sums paid to charitable institutions, a man, to take an illustration, might- reduce his income tax by $10,000. That $10,000

belongs to the people of Canada. He would very likely if he were prompted to give aid to a charitable institution give it to an institution in his own town. Thus he would be taking the money of the people of Canada and giving it to the people of his own city or town. It is not a formidable objection but it is an objection I think.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization
speechtext: I might mention another illustration along the same line, that came up for discussion this morning in another way. In the province of Saskatchewan, for example, our municipalities pay the entire cost of hospitals; the hospital management does not appeal to the public at all. The burden of carrying the expenditure in connection with our hospitals is always borne by the people as a whole in the way of taxation. Consequently there are no contributions of this kind to charitable institutions of that nature. But I understand, for example, that in the city of Toronto the hospitals there are maintained to a very large extent by private contributions. Well, why should a man in Toronto be partially exempt from his income tax if he makes contributions to an institution there, Whereas in 'Saskatchewan our people do not make contributions of that kind to the hospitals and have to bear the whole income tax. You will find all sorts of such anomalous situations. I think the illustration given by the hon. gentleman who has just spoken should not apply unless the charitable institution is national in its scope and has national work to do. Otherwise I think you will have all sorts of anomalies in the working out of a provision of that kind.

If the people of Saskatchewan escape 'claims for a hospital they are called upon to make good in other respects. I do not imagine that among the many inducements that are offered to people to settle in that province we could hold out to them the expectation that they would not have toi contribute to charities; in one form or another they will get at them.
, Another point occurs to me. Let me say that I think nine men out of ten who1 will claim an exemption of this kind can be trusted to make an . honest return. I think the cases in which this privilege would be used to evade the law are very few indeed. The man who gives liberally to these institutions is not the man who is likely to make a false income tax return.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I entirely agree with my hon. friend. It is not the man who does the right thing who. is likely to evade the Act. It is the man who would

not give anything at all to charity, and he is the one that I want to look after.

I think possibly the
amendment could be modified so as to cover cases where the grant is made to an institution that is recognized by the State. As drafted the amendment possibly leaves the door too wide open and would cover an organization which would not really be recognized as a charity. But I think that if the Government took the clause under their consideration the sense of the House is largely to the effect that in the case of charities that are recognized by law a man might be allowed to make contributions Which would be free from the income tax. With respect to the province of Saskatchewan they, of course, are starting out new and are beginning in the right way by making the State take care of all their charitable work of that kind. Unfortunately, however, in the province of Ontario, and the other older provinces, the old system of a man bequeathing money to charity in his will, and of the public sup porting these charities to a large extent by individual contributions, prevails. In Ontario there are hospitals in every town of any size which hospitals are maintained by grants from the province and from the local municipality, and largely by contributions from kind-hearted people. The same system obtains in the province of Quebec, and the amount of revenue that will be lost to the Government through this exemption would be very small. In the case of the Sick Children's Hospital in Toronto, unless there was ail exemption the institution would lose something like forty or fifty thousand dollars a year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It would not turn on this at all.
Mr. 'CURRIE: At the same time I think the clause should be changed so as to cover a case of that kind. I would suggest that rather than have the matter voted on and encounter any trouble-seeing that we are all concerned in doling the best we can ta meet the situation-the Government should reconsider the clause and see if the proposed amendment cannot be so changed that the door would not be left open too wide, and have it so that if an individual makes contributions at all he should contribute to a national charity.

I think if the minister and the member for London would spend a few minutes together they would reach a conclusion, and I for one would willingly submit to their judgment.
Clause stands.

subsection 5 is .to cover the case of such men as mining engineeis who, having their address outside of .Canada, spend five or six months of their time in this country and derive a very substantial income from work which they do here. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Most of these
men return to Canada. But there is a great deal in my hon. friend's suggestion; we will see what can be done in the matter.

A large number of men in Canada who constitute our floating population are, I believe, entirely escaping the income tax. I want to be specific; I will refer to the part of the country in which I live. Employers of labour in the newer parts of Canada are asked to furnish to the department a list of all their employees who earn the equivalent of $1,000 a year and who work in Canada for six months or longer at a time. This means a very considerable burden on the employer in the keeping of records, and my judgment is that the department is getting nothing as a result in the way of revenue, because these men are moving around from place to place in such a way that the income tax collector cannot catch up with them. Some of the people, returned soldiers, for instance, feel that they are not being justly treated in this matter. We have a large number of foreigners in Northern Ontario. Recently I happened to be in a bank in a town in Northern Ontario. Two foreigners came in to draw out their money before going home to the old country; between them they had accumulated over $7,000. A returned soldier who was standing by said to me: "Is it fair that ihese men should wholly escape taxation while we who have just come back from the war and are getting into employment are being taxed on our incomes over $1,000?" What answer could I give? I made a suggestion to the department, and I give it now to the committee for what it is worth: that these employers, instead of being asked to send in elaborate returns giving the names of foreigners whom they would not know on the street if they met them, be called upon [Sir Henry Drayton.1
to collect the tax out of the wages of such classes of employees as I have indicated. That may seem a drastic method of collecting the tax on a man's income. But I submit that if these people are to be reached at all some means of that kind will have to be adopted; otherwise they will go on earning substantial incomes, as they have been year after year, without contributing a nickel to the national revenue.
Do I understand my hon. friend to mean that these men should have paid a tax on the amount which they withdrew from the bank?
No, I do not meant that.
They may have earned less than $1,000 a year.

Well, if they did, they should not be taxed, but the majority of them earn much more than that and are escaping taxation. I am prepared to say that 10,000 men between the Ottawa river and the boundary line between Manitoba and Ontario who are earning more than $1,000 a year are wholly escaping income taxation simply because no method has so far been adopted of collecting from them. I have no method to suggest, unless you catch them at the time that they are receiving their wages.

You w'ould have to say to the ordinary labourer who works thirty days in one place and fifteen in another: "You are earning so much per day, which is so much more than $1,000 a year," and then you would have to force the employer to collect the money for the Government.

I wish to support the remarks of my hon. friend (Mr. G. B. Nicholson). In my city a great deal of piece work has been going on during the last few years, and it has been the complaint of the people there that many men of outside or alien nationalities were earning large wages on piece work, even as high as $10, $15, and $20 a day, and contributing to this country absolutely nothing by way of income tax. I wish to support the remarks of my hon. friend (Mr. G. B. Nicholson) in that regard, because I think his remarks are well worth considering by the Minister of Finance as a new method of securing revenue for the Dominion treasury from men of this kind.
The machinery is hard to work.

There is a great deal of truth in what my hon. friend (Mr. G. B. Nicholson) has stated. Many foreigners are coming into this country and earning large wages, and they are, to a large extent, doing what the hon. member has stated. While they are in this country they spend practically nothing; they save up their money and they send their savings to the country from which they came, thus getting out of paying one cent of taxes or contributing in any way to the upkeep of this country. In the constituency which I have the honour to represent there are many Mexicans who earn large wages, who live on practically nothing and who send their savings back to their own country, thus evading any-responsibility for the upkeep of this country. The hon. member is not trying to find any fault; he is suggesting that this is a matter that should be looked into seriously by the Government, and if we can get a revenue from this source, I am satisfied that every hon. member will heartily approve such action on the part of the Government.

speechtext:
That may be,
but we feel that it is important that the money should be paid at the earliest possible moment and that the department should not waste a lot of time determining what the real income is.

I see a difficulty in the direction indicated by the hon. member for Three Rivers. A man will he obliged to be his own assessor in this matter and very many men will not be able to determine what their taxable income is. The hon. minister says that there must be an investigation, and that very fact shows that the innocent taxpayer himself may be in doubt. I agree that once a man has received his bill the sooner you can get the money the better. But the ordinary man will have some difficulty in deciding what his taxable income is. He will put items in one way or the other which the department may not approve of. How is he to know what his actual tax is until he gets his bill? I sympathize with the minister in his desire to get the money as quickly as possible and to reduce the labour of the tax gathering authorities, who will have a troublesome job, but at the same time there is something in the criticism of the hon. member for Three Rivers, and until a man has received his tax bill I do not see how he can make a payment on account.
Mr. DuTRJEMBLAY: I think the contention of the hon. member for Three Rivers and the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's is absolutely correct. Under the present law it is extremely difficult for ordinary ffeople to determine the amount they have to pay each year. The collectors will t-ell you that in Montreal thousands of people are faced with this difficulty and want to know what this or the other item means, and there is great room for error and misunderstanding. I think that the Government should send the bill to the taxpayer. It is very unfair to put the people in such a position as to be liable to a penalty if they do not pay up within a certain time, when they have no means of properly complying with the law.
The tax for 1919 has not been paid. Have the statements been sent out to the people?	<

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

Are they supposed to
send in those statements in accordance with the clause?

Sir 'HENRY DRAYTON: No; this section does not come into force until next year.
It applies to 1920.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It applies to incomes received in 1920 which are to be returned in 1921.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext: The situation is somewhat complicated by the multiplicity of taxes. For instance, there is an allowance for business profits tax and also an allowance in regard to taxes already collected on dividends. If there were only one tax, the income tax, the matter would he simpler, and it would be sound business for the debtor at once to make payment. But the minister himself, by the multiplicity of taxes, is going to make the situation difficult; and later on, before the clause passes, I shall direct his attention to the question of penalties. It seems to me that the penalties are rather extreme in view of the dangers which threaten people who may innocently make mistakes in rendering their accounts. Even the minister realizes this, because he anticipates, according to the clause, that there will he many bankruptcies on account of this taxation and he makes provision for such cases. This clause needs revision.

I observe that in his Budget Speech the minister says that in all cases where it is discovered that over-payment has been made by the ratepayer, a refund for the amount must be immediately made to him or applied on any instalment due or becoming due. This would to a considerable extent relieve the severity of the law now under discussion; but so far as I can see, no cognizance has been taken of this statement in the legislation we are now considering.

Might not the minister allow this clause to stand? There will be many objections from different members of the House to its passing, and the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's and the hon. member for Three Rivers have already expressed opinions which the minister should take into consideration. I think the minister might let it stand.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Until eight o'clock.

A certain questionnaire is now sent out and questions are to be answered by the taxpayer. That form is sent back and the rest of the work is done by the department. The amount is ascertained and the bill is sent to the taxpayer. 'Speaking for myself, I should think that it would

be better to continue that form. The people in the last two or three years have become accustomed to it, and I would suggest to the minister that he stand by the old method of having the amount ascertained in the department and sending the bill direct to the individual. I venture to say that this new proposal is only duplicating the work; hardly one man in a hundred will be able to ascertain the proper amount he has to pay, and it may be discovered in the long run that the whole thing is wrong and has to be done over again. I do not say that any taxpayer will intentionally give a wrong return, but this will happen, and the department will discover that there are errors and a duplication of work, and possibly the taxpayer will be subject to a fine because he innocently failed to make a correct return. I seriously bring this matter to the consideration of the minister, and would suggest that the amount be ascertained by the department itself. After the department has obtained the facts it can send the bill direct to the man. As to what terms the department may make with the taxpayer as to instalments and so forth, that is a matter for their consideration. I do say that the amount of the bill should be ascertained when the proper machinery is present for ascertaining it.

The minister might make it plainer for the people if he put on the margin of the form a table showing the tax. Most people have not the statutes before them. Some of the banks have published a little pamphlet with a scale showing what the tax would amount to on certain incomes and that is very handy. Many people have not got that. When the minister is making a new form it would be easy to put on the margin something that would let people know the amounts that they would have to pay. That is all the more necessary owing to the fact that the minister is asking the people to advance 25 per cent of the tax when making their return.

It strikes me that in the end it would be much more satisfactory if the minister would continue having the returns made as they have been made. Let the taxpayer, when he is .sending in his return to be approved, send in 25 per cent of the approximate amount and then make the tax due and payable after the return has been passed upon by the department.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Twenty-five per cent cash?

Twenty-five per cent in cash and the balance after it has been passed upon by the department.
Progress reported.
At Six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess.
The House resumed at Eight o'clock.
