speechtext:
Hon. HUGH GUTHRIE (Acting Solicitor General) moved the second reading of Bill No. 126 to amend the Bankruptcy Act. He said:	«
The House is aware that during the first session of 1919 a Bankruptcy Act was passed by this Parliament. That Act did not go into force at the passing thereof hut by its provisions was to go into force upon proclamation being made therefor by the Governor General in Council. Early in the present session the proclamation was issued bringing the Bankruptcy Act into force on the 1st of July next. The Act itself is rather a comprehensive measure and somewhat intricate. One object in allowing <a lapse of time between the passage of the Act and its coming into operation was to give the people .an opportunity of understanding it, and during the past year there have been certain criticisms levelled at it. A number of suggestions have been received from Chambers of Oommeroe, from mercantile 'associations, from judges and from Bar Associations suggesting certain amendments which had not occurred to 'any member of the House when the Bill wias in committee last year. These have now been examined and passed upon by the law officers of the Grown, and it is felt that a number of them should be incorporated in the Act (for the purpose of simplifying and making it generally more workable. It (would be a difficult thing on a motion for the second reading of the Bill to discuss these matters as they appear in the Bill itself-they are somewhat technical,-but most of the amendments I think 207
are ralther clerical than otherwise. I would ask the House to pass the second reading and allow the Bill to go into committee when the various . amendments proposed can be more fully explained.
Motion agreed to and Bill read the second time, and the House went into committee on the Bill, Mr. Steele in the Chair.
On section 2-"debtor."

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: The only change made by clause 2 as printed in the Bill is to insert the words, " except by leave of the court " in line 21, and also the words, " or afterwards by leave of the court" in line 25. The reason- for the amendment is simply this., By the Act passed last session all corporations were placed under the jurisdiction of the Bankruptcy Act for the purpose of winding up. It has been suggested that some of the provisions of the old Winding-Up Act, as to assets and as to the rights of creditors and the rights of contributories, might in some rather indefinite cases be useful for the court in settling the assets of an estate or the rights of contributories. It hae been suggested by some of the judges of Canada that if any of these special cases should arise, by leave of the court the aid of these clauses in the Winding-Up Act might he invoked under the Bankruptcy Act, but it would only be in special cases, and therefore the words inserted in the amendment are, "except by leave of the court." I see no objection to the amendment, though personally I thought the section was good enough as it stood.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Amendment agreed to, and section as amended agreed to.
On section 3-" Locality

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
The only change in that is with regard to the term of six months during which the debtor carries on business. In the Act as passed the language was:	,


within a bankruptcy division or district where at the debtor has carried on business for the longest period during the six months immediately preceding the date of the presentation against him of a bankruptcy petition.
The proposal now is to strike out the words, " for the longest period during the six months " and insert the words, " whereat the debtor has carried on business at any time during the said six months immediately preceding the date of the presentation against him of a bankruptcy petition."
It may be hard to ascertain just where an insolvent debtor has carried on business for the longest period during the last six



months, and it has been suggested it would make it more definite if the enactment were in the form suggested by this amendment.

Have the bankruptcy
divisions or districts been established by the Government?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I am under the impression that they have. The operation of the Act is now under the Department of the Secretary of State. I have discussed the matter with the Under-Secretary of State, who is very familiar with the whole matter, and my information is that the rules have been prescribed, the bankruptcy divisions established, and I think probably the list of trustees has been more or less completed; I do not think it is finally completed, and will not be, until this amending Act is passed. My information is that all the machinery is well under way for the coming into force of the Act on the 1st of July next.

The proclamation has
been issued?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
Were the districts created by that proclamation?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: No, they are prescribed by rules and regulations.

Will these rules and
regulations be printed and distributed before tbe 1st of July next?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
They are practically
ready for distribution; I think my hon. friend could get a copy of them to-morrow. They will be. slightly amended in consequence of these amendments.

These rules have been
made by the Undersecretary of State?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
|By the Governor in
Council.
In order that they shall come into operation is it not necessary that they shall be submitted to the approval of Parliament?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: No, I do not think that is necessary.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 4-affidavit:

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
In the original Act this section reads as follows:
The petition shall be verified by affidavit of the creditor or of some person on his behalf having knowledge of the facts.

The manner of the service and the manner of the verifying are prescribed by the rules; it is considered that the amendment is better drafting than the clause as originally drawn.

But these rules may be
changed by the Governor in Council?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, the rules of practice may be changed.

And the Governor in
Council may change the procedure in connection with the affidavit? Would it not be preferable to leave the clause as it stands? Why leave this question of procedure to the Governor in Council?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
The memorandum
which I have says that the judges who have gone over the Bill suggest that we do not change the old form prescribed in the Winding-Up Act-a form which has been in force in this country for thirty or forty years.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 5-proceedings taken in wrong court:

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Subsection (11) is a
new provision. The proceedings should not be nullified, simply because a man files his petition in the wrong court. In this provision the court is given power in such a case to transfer the proceedings to the proper court.

I assume that " wrong
court " would mean a court without jurisdiction?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
The right court would
be the court having jurisdiction. The judge in bankruptcy would have the right to transfer the proceedings to the proper court.
He should have not only the right but the obligation.

I am not a master of
the English language, but it seems strange ' that the expression "wrong court " should be used. Why not say, " a court not having jurisdiction?"

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
The petition might be
filed in a court having jurisdiction in the province of Quebec whereas it should have been filed in a court in Ontario. The words " wrong court " here mean, I think, courts which are not bankruptcy courts; I think they are intended to cover any court; if a petition is filed in the Supreme Court of

Ontario and should not be there, it may be transferred to the proper court.
air. ARCHAMBAULT:	Does it mean
that if the proceedings are instituted in Ontario they .may be transferred to the province of Quebec?,

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
The bankruptcy judge
would have that power. Bankruptcy courts are federal, not provincial courts.
'Section agreed to.
On section 6-receiving orders and assignments to take precedence of attachments, executions, etc.:

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
This is a rather peculiar change, but it is one which I do not think objection can be taken. In the Act as passed we had a provision at the end of subsection (1) which was inserted having regard to the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, although it did, not name them. In those two provinces a different practice obtains from that prevailing in the other provinces in regard to judgment debts. There judgments are looked upon as securities; a man taking a judgment will keep it in force for a great number of years, keeping it more as a mortgage than as a judgment, and obtaining annually his interest from the debtor. I understand that a good deal of money is thus invested in those two provinces, and to protect such judgments the House inserted this provision in the Act of last session:
Provided that this paragraph shall not apply to any execution or other process issued against real or immovable property under or by virtue of a judgment registered prior to the coming into operation of this Act, which judgment, as the result of such registration, became, under the laws of the province wherein it was entered a charge, lien or hypothec upon or of such real or immovable property.
It has been suggested that this provision be struck out and that a clause be inserted in the terms of clause 7 of the Bill now before us, limiting the application of that provision to Nova Scotia and New Brunswick.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section'8-avoidance of preference in certain cases:

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
This clause has a history. In the form in which it appears in the Bill before the committee, it was practically in the Bill which went before the special committee in the spring session of 1919. It is an embodiment of the Ontario statute, and I think it is the law if not in 207i
all, in many of the provinces of the Dominion of Canada. The special committee which dealt with the Bill in 1919 saw fit to change it, and we thought we had improved it. When it came before the House it was passed in the farm in which the committee submitted it. When, however, it came before the Senate, it was again amended in the form in which it now appears in the Bankruptcy Act. As it appears in the enactment of to-day it is the law neither of the province of Ontario nor of any of the other provinces. There is no great variation, I am bound to say; hut there are some slight changes in language in this clause which is one of the important clauses of the Bill, and I think the result will be that .all judicial decisions which we have had the benefit of in Canada heretofore will not apply to this section as passed by the House last session. Consequently, those who take a deep interest in this measure have come to the conclusion that it would be far wiser to adopt the Ontario law upon the subject which is, as I say, the law in a majority of the provinces of Canada at the present time. The amendment now proposed is practically an adoption of the Ontario clause. It does not make much change in the clause as originally passed; it strikes out these words:
If made, incurred, paid, taken, or suffered, with such view as aforesaid.
That is, with a view of giving a preference. It inserts subclause 2 in the Bill before the committee:
If any such conveyance, transfer, payment, obligation or judicial proceeding has the effect of giving any creditor a preference over other creditors, or over any one or more of them, it shall be presumed prima facie to have been made, incurred, taken, paid or suffered with such view as aforesaid whether or not it was made voluntarily or under pressure and. evidence of pressure shall not be receivable or avail to support such transaction.
Where such a transaction as that is impeached, it shall be presumed prima facie to have been a preferential transaction and consequently, void as against a trustee in bankruptcy.
Void, ipso facto?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Not as between the parties, but only as against the trustee having a prior claim. I think it is wise to put in the well-understood clause of so many provinces and so to remove any doubt which may exist by virtue of the Senate's amendment of last year. *

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext:
The minister would not care to alter the clause to this extent, that if a

party who secured a mortgage had delivered goods within, say sixty days of the demand for bankruptcy, then the mortgage or guarantee might stand good?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I do not quite understand the question. Three months is the term limit of the clause. Your six months' mortgage, if not fraudulent, if a bona fide transaction, would be good.
But nothing prevents a trustee, even if the transaction be of older date, to prove fraudulent intent?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: It might be fraudulent, no matter how old it is. There is no question of the presumption.
There is no bar to proving fradulent intent?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Not at all.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 9-recovery:

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
The change in this clause is very slight. Under the Act as passed under the circumstances stated, the section provided that-
The trustee may, with the approval of the inspectors of the estate, institute in a court having jurisdiction in debt to such amount, an action or other proceedings for the recovery thereof.
This clause is much simpler; it reads:
If at the expiration of thirty days from the date of the service of such demand the contributory has not paid to the trustee the required amount, the trustee may take proceedings against the contributory for the recovery thereof in the manner provided by General Rules.
The distinction is this. The manner provided by general rules will be in a bankruptcy court. In the Act as passed, the proceedings could be taken in any court of competent jurisdiction. It has been thought that bankruptcy matters should he dealt with, in soi far as possible, in a single court, in a federal court, and if a contributory is ordered to pay money and does not pay it, the trustee would go to the bankruptcy court in order to take proceedings.

May I be permitted to ask the minister a question in regard to section 31, which reads:
Every conveyance or transfer of property or charge thereon made, every payment made-
And so forth? Supposing a man conveys a transfer by way of mortgage to another man who may be a creditor and the latter advances him more money, what position would that creditor be in?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I am afraid that would be regarded as a preferential claim and wo'uld be set aside. If the transaction is made " with a view of giving such creditor a preference over other creditors" or has the effect of doing so, "if the person making, incurring, taking, paying or suffering the same is adjudged bankrupt on a bankruptcy petition presented within three months after the date of making, incurring, taking, paying or suffering the same," the same shall be adjudged a preference.
That is going a pretty long way.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I think that is the law in my hon. friend's own province.
Only as regards personal . property, not real estate. It has that effect in the case of a bill of sale, but not in the case of a mortgage.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I do not see any reason 'for the distinction between a mortgage and a bill of sale. Property is property, and creditors have the right to get after it. I do not see why it should1 be impeached in the one case and not in the other. I know that in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick they have laws more or less favourable to creditors in regard to real estate. Those judgments which I spoke of a few moments ago are but instances of that. I think the proper principle is to place all creditors as far as possible on an equal footing, and to abolish as far as we can all preferences between them.

The difficulty will be this. A man might be a creditor and someone in need of money may go to this same creditor and borrow $5,000 giving a mortgage on real estate for security. The creditor has the title searched, finds it is all correct, and takes the mortgage. The real estate is clear of all encumbrances so far as he knows. He advances the $5,000 to enable the man to carry on the business and at the end of three months he may be out the $5,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: He would not -lose it; he would be an ordinary creditor for it.

He would only rank with the other creditors irrespective of his security.
I am afraid it would have the effect of interfering with legitimate business.

Are these General
Rules referred to in subsection 8 new rules that are to be passed? Why should not the minister adopt the practice in the different provinces? In Ontario, for instance, they have the Judicature Act, just

as we have in Nova Scotia, and a well-established .practice, and the same is true of all the other provinces. It would be rather awkward for a man who is getting well up in years like my-self to have to learn a new procedure and practice. The Judicature Adt is the procedure in ia.ll the courts in England, and I do not see why it should not be applicable in collecting .a debt in this court.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: The Judicature Act is not the practice in bankruptcy proceedings in England. The rules there are just as we propose to pass them here. My hon. friend was probably present in the House last year when that question was raised, and - he will remember there was a pretty full discussion on it. One reason for passing these rules is to simplify the practice and make it uniform -throughout the whole of Canada. At the- present time -we have different forms oif practice in the courts of the various provinces of the Dominion'. A man may wish to- invoke the -aid of a bankruptcy court in British Columbia, and may reside in Nova Scotia. There is only one petition, only one procedure. The- id-ea ha,s been to make this as simple as possible, and ito make it uniform. I lam satisfied that my hon. friend (Mr. McKenzie) will have no difficulty in following this practice. I -took the opportunity a -few -days -ago of reading -through the practice, and I -think it much -more simple than.- any practice we hav-e in ithe Ontario courts. I think the chief thing to he gained is uniformity and simplicity. Thi-s, I think, will be obtained in- the rules when they are issued. They have been printed and are practically complete. There may be one or two- changes necessary in consequence of these amendments, -but otherwise I iam assured by the Under-Secretary of State they -are about ready for distribution.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 10-distribution of estate of bankrupt after notice:
-Mr. GUTHRIE:	There is a very slight
change in this section. The note I have on it is that this amendment is asked merely to correct a mistake in the wording which crept into the Act of last year. So far as I can find out the only change is that they have inserted the words at line 43 "as provided by section 42, subsection 2 of this Act," and in line 46 they have used the Word "regulations" instead of the word "notice." I think these are simply clerical errors, and I do not see any objection to them all.
Section agreed to.
On section 11-not to exceed 5 per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: This clause was suggested by my hon. friend (Mr. J-acobs). It deals with the question of remuneration of trustees. -Certain representations -have been made to the -Government that the absolute limitation of a trustee's fee to 5 per cent in every case would undoubtedly work a hardship in some .eases, particularly where the assets were small and the amount of work to be performed by the trustee was abnormally large. It has always been the custom in -Canada for the creditors themselves or the inspectors to decide on the amount of the trustee's fees, in cas-es where the trustee asks for more than 5 per cent. This practice we think should continue except in oases where the trustee is able to pay the creditors one hundred cents on the dollar, in which case the debtor would have an equity and the court should then decide. As the Bill pasi-ed last session 5 per cent was the limitation in all cases, great and small. We deliberately took it out of the hands of the creditors. It has been pointed out to us, how ver, that in oases of small estates 5 per cent may he too small a fee. The proposed amendment will leave it in the hands of the creditors and inspectors- I think it is only the creditors-to fix the amount in the case of small estates.

This section does not seem to show that the creditors are going to fix the amount of indemnity to be paid the trustees.
-Mr. GUTHRIE:	We have -another section on that. This is merely striking out that 5 per cent limitation.
-Section agreed to.
On section 12-inspectors' fees.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
The former enactment provided that each inspector might he paid his actual and necessary travelling expenses "in and about the performance of his duties, and such sums only." The committee that threshed this matter out and also the committee of the House were inclined to think that the inspectors should be paid actual expenses. That was the view of the House when the Bill went through, and we so provided. 'However, this is the suggestion of my hon. friend- from George Etienne -Cartier (Mr. Jacobs), and after giving the matter fuller consideration than was given it last year I have come to the conclusion that the proposal is not unreasonable. It fixes a fairly modest fee for inspectors, having regard to the amount of the estate, and I arranged with my hon. friend that I would

take no exception to the clause being introduced. It was introduced in a public Bill brought forward by my hon. friend at the beginning of the session.

Is there anything in the Bill to limit the number of meetings that can be held? I followed the Bill closely last year but I do not remember its terms. Some unscrupulous man might have too many meetings.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I do not know that there is any actual limitation. Clause 42, which is rather lengthy, provides for the meetings that are to be held. The first meeting shall be held immediately after assignment and subsequent meetings may be called at any time by the trustee if he is requested to do so by a certain number of creditors. I do not see any power for inspectors to call meetings; that power rests in the hands of the trustees and creditors.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 13-proofs of debts.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
The old section is very much like this. It reads:
Every creditor shall prove his debt as soon as may be after the making of a receiving order or after the date of an authorized assignment.
. Mr. PARENT: Is there any form of procedure provided in regard to evidence?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: He just makes his affidavit. A majority of the creditors may dispute his claim and, of course, he will have to prove it in court.
"As soon as may be" is rather vague, is it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I think not; it means as soon as possible or convenient. You cannot very well impose a time limit on a creditor, because he may not be in the country. You have to be reasonably careful of the claims of creditors. So long as the estate has not been actually distributed a creditor may come in under the Act we passed last year. The object is to expedite the matter as much as possible and get all creditors before the trustee at the earliest possible moment.
Is there no time limit?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Not for the proving of a claim. If the estate has been distributed then, of course, the creditor's claim is barred.
Is there any provision limiting the time in regard to the distribution of the estate?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: There is.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 14-partners and separate estates.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
The change here is in the last clause. Subsection (3) reads:
If there is a surplus of the joint estate, it shall be dealt with as part of the respective separate estates in proportion to the right and interest of each partner in the joint estate.
The section as passed last year read:
If there is a surplus of the separate estate, it shall be dealt with as part of the respective separate estates in proportion to the right and interest of each partner in the joint estate.
We have just reversed it.

A man may be a bankrupt in connection with a business in which he was a partner, and might be solvent as regards his own private business. Personally he is responsible for any debts incurred in connection with his own private business, but as a partner in a business he is responsible only in so far as the business is responsible. How do you treat that situation?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I quite understand the question. The defect in the section as printed was due to the fact that the printer left three 'lines out, and I was not aware of that fact until I looked at my memorandum which the Undersecretary of State prepared. He says that the object of this amendment is merely to insert three lines omitted by the printer. I think that the languages of subsection (3) answers my hon. friend much better than I can answer him.
In the case of partners the joint estate shall be applicable in the first instance in the payment of their joint debts, and the separate estate of each partner shall be applicable in the first instance in payment of his separate debts.
That is the declaration of the common law. If after using the separate estate a man still has money left it can go to pay the partnership debts.
Even in the case of a limited business?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I am not familiar with limited partnerships. There is a law in Ontario permitting limited partnerships, but I have not heard of one.

There is a law in regard to limited partnerships in Quebec also. In Quebec, the partner is only liable for the amount of money he agrees to contribute, and nothing further. He is merely like a

stockholder in an ordinary joint stock company, and I assume that this law will not interfere with that rule. When the partnership is registered, notice is given to the commercial public that the limited partner is liable only for a certain sum and nothing further, and I presume that he could not be held under this section for any further sum.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: This section would not hold him liable.
That is the point I had in mind.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 15-penalty for failure to attend for examination.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: There is only one change; in the eleventh line of the old Act, the word "debtor" is changed to the word "him." But rather than have the section amended we repeal it and put in an entirely new section, so that when the Act comes into force it may have as few small amendments as possible.
Is the punishment of twelve monflfes the same as under the English Bankruptcy Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not know. We
threshed these penalties out pretty well when we passed this particular section last year, but I do not know whether it is the same as the English Act. I am inclined to think it is.

Is the party who fails
' to appear treated as a criminal or does the person at whose instance he is put into jail contribute to his maintenance?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I think he would be
treated as any other prisoner in the jail; his maintenance would be paid for by the municipal or provincial authorities. His imprisonment would be imprisonment for contempt of court.

In our practice in the province of Quebec-I am not familiar with the practice in the other provinces, although I was iSolicitor General for a time- in a case of contempt of court, say, or of action for damages, the court may declare that a certain sum be paid or in default the person be sent to jail. A debtor remains in jail so long as a stated sum per week is paid by the creditor. If the creditor fails* to pay for the maintenance of the prisoner; who is placed in what is known as the debtors' ward, the debtor walks out and is free. Is it the same in this case when the debtor fails to appear after being ordered to do so?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I would not think so. The law which my hon. friend speaks of was at one time in force in England, but that was many years ago. I do not believe that that law was ever in force in Ontario; at any Tate, not in my time.

It is still in force in
Quebec.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I remember a discussion on that point last year, and in certain actions for damage in that province, I believe, a man can be imprisoned. But in this section the man would be punishable for contempt of court for refusing to obey the summons of the court, and his maintenance would be at the expense of the municipal or provincial authorities.

If in the meantime the
debtor shows his willingness to give satisfactory answers to the questions, could he not by application be brought before the court and, after having given those answers, be freed? That is to say, as we say in Quebec law, if he purges himself of his offense, would he not be released forthwith? That would be the rule under contempt of court proceedings in our province.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Under this provision he has a fairly good remedy in his own hands. If he refuses to attend and give evidence they have to summon him and bring him up again, so that he has ample opportunity.
Then after his second refusal:
-the court may, by warrant, cause him to be apprehended and brought up for examination-
He may first of all be brought up for examination.
-and may order him to be committed to the common gaol of the judicial district in which he resides for any term not exceeding twelve months.
Supposing the debtor has seen the error of his ways after serving six months?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: He may make application for clemency.
Application to the executive clemency of the Solicitor General? May the Lord have mercy on his soul!

Reading beyond line
20 there seems to be some doubt as to the protection afforded to one who refuses to answer a question. It is well known that if a man is asked a question which tends to incriminate him, he is not bound to answer it. There seems to be a statement

here to the effect that if there 9 p.m. is any impediment in the way of producing a book or an account he is excusable. I think it is very doubtful if that applies to a man who refuses to answer a question. It is not sufficiently plain to me that if he has any excuse for refusing to answer a question he is excused, whereas if there is any impediment in the way of producing a book or an account he will be excused. The general rule is that a man is not obliged in a civil proceeding to answer any question that tends to incriminate him.
Or in a criminal proceeding.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
The section covers the
point raised by my hon. friend Mr. McKenzie if he will read it carefully. The section reads from line 20 on:
-or, if attending, refuses to make satisfactory answers to any questions asked him or refuses to produce any book, document or other paper.
There is a comma.
-having no lawful impediment made known to the examiner at the time of his sitting for such examination and allowed by him.
I think that qualification applies to his refusal to answer a question as well as his refusal to produce a book or paper. I think that the word " impediment " would cover either ground of privilege that a witness might urge.

If the minister thinks it is clear that " impediment " is common to both grounds, of course I will be satisfied, but I never saw the word " impediment " used as an excuse for not answering a question. There might be an " impediment " in the way of producing a book- some one else might have the book and the witness might not be able to get it-but the use of the word " impediment " as applied to a condition under which he may refuse to answer a question is new legal phraseology to me.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: If it is an impediment recognized by law a man would be able to claim privilege under it.

Does not the Acting Solicitor General think it would be wise, in view of the importance of the question to be decided under the section, to insert a declaration that nothing in section 15 shall take away the right given by the Criminal Code to any person who claims to be allowed not to answer a question on the ground that it might incriminate him?

Mr. GUTHRIE.:	I think the Criminal
Code itself would do that.
These are two statutes side by side.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
The language is taken
directly from the English Act.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 16-solicitors' and witness fees.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
In the clause of the Act which was passed last session we provided:
All attorneys, solicitors '<nd counsel acting for the trustee or for the estate of a debtor in respect of proceedings under this Act, shall be paid out of the assets of such estate their reasonable costs and fees as fixed in a tariff provided by General Rules; but, except as hereinafter provided, the aggregate amount of such costs and fees so payable out of the assets of estates whereof the gross proceeds exceed five thousand dollars shall not exceed five per centum of such gross proceeds.
We have struck out the "five per centum" and the "gross proceeds."
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
My hon. friend says,
"Hear, hear." Well, this is at his own suggestion. I think the amendment is a good one and I have no hesitation in saying the committee ought to accept it.

When the Bill left this
House last year the section was pretty much in the shape proposed in the amendment, but when the Bill came back from the Senate it had this objectionable clause which we are now seeking to remove.
Section as amended agreed to.
The 'CHAIRMAN:	Section 17-undischarged bankrupt obtaining credit.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Before you read that
section may I asik the committee to consider these sections:	Since the Bill was
introduced two very eminent judges of Canada have suggested two sections. One is an amendment to section 65 as to the powers of the registrar of the court. They merely ask to add this clause:
Any person dissatisfied with an order or decision of the Registrar may appeal therefrom to a Judge in the manner prescribed by General Rules.
I do net see any very great objection to that. Another amendment I may mention '.now is to section 71, as to the enforcement of Orders of Court throughout Canada. It has been suggested that clause 3 be added there:
The court may direct any issue to be tried or inquiry to be made by any judge or officer of

any of the Courts of the Province and the decision of such judge or officer shall be subject to appeal to a judge in bankruptcy, unless the judge is not a judge of a Superior Court when the appeal shall be under section 74 of this Act.
That is a matter of convenience. If, for convenience, in any case, it is deemed proper to refer any particular questions to the decision of a judge, even if he be not a judge of bankruptcy, such a course may be pursued. I should not have thought the suggestions were essential to the proper carrying out of the Act but as both of the judges who have made them are, in the provinces where they reside, of the very highest reputation, I think perhaps the Act might be improved if these amendments were included. If the committee is willing I will move them.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Mr. Guthrie moves
that section 65 of the said Act be hereby amended by adding thereto subsection 4.
I suppose that would mean that if the trustee or receiver is dissatisfied with the decision of the registrar he may also appeal.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I think that is broad enough to include anybody. I may say that Mr. Justice Middleton, of the Ontario Superior Court, and Mr. Justice Maclennan, of Montreal, have gone very carefully over the Act and these amendments are brought here at their suggestion. They think the amendments will greatly improve the working of the Act. '
Amendment agreed to and section as amended agreed to.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Mr. Guthrie now moves that section 71 of the said Act be amended by adding thereto subsection 3. Shall this amendment carry?

I think that rule might very well apply to the provinces outside the province of Quebec, but it seems to me unreasonable that judges of courts of inferior jurisdiction should be asked to try any of these questions in bankruptcy. For instance I may point out-

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: It is only where the judge of a bankruptcy court would direct, and I think such a judge would be very careful about whom he should refer a question to. In the meantime I would not hesitate to trust them with the power.

What I wish to point out is this: The province of Quebec is divided into seventeen or eighteen districts in each of which a judge of the Superior Court site.
Now we also have judges of the inferior courts who try cases under $100. It would not be well to have these judges of inferior courts pass upon questions of bankruptcy at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I quite agree with my hon. friend, but I think the way the matter will work out is that in each province a judge or judges will be designated to attend to bankruptcy matters, and I have no doubt they will be very careful with the administration of this law.
Will there be one judge for an entire province?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: There may be one or more. One may be sufficient at first, but as time goes on more than one may be required. I can understand that where a number of minor .applications come up for decision a judge may find it necessary to refer something, but I think he will be very careful as to whom he refers it to. We may as well see it tried out and if any wrong results, at the next session of Parliament we can change the law.
Are there to be special judges appointed for the .administration of this Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
No, the judges of the superior court are charged with the administration of the Act, but as between themselves I believe that in arranging their judicial duties they are going to make the apportionment in such a way that, to as large an extent as possible, one or two judges shall deal with bankruptcy matters, for the beginning at all events, until we get a uniform practice.
Amendment agreed to and section as amended agreed to.
On section 17-undischarged bankrupt obtaining credit:

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: was entirely too large an amount to fix; that if he ran an account of $60 or $100, under such circumstances, he should be liable to heavy penalties for doing so. It was for that reason that the amount was reduced from $500 to $50. I have no particular view on the subject, but I do think that the running of an account up to so small an amount as '$50 should hardly render such a man liable to a year's imprisonment. Of course, he is guilty of concealing a most material fact, because if he did disclose to the dealer that he was an undischarged bankrupt he would not get the credit. I think that $500 is too high and that $50 is rather low. However, I shall be guided by the view of the committee. 1

The Acting Solicitor General will remember how vigorously we on this side opposed this clause when it was presented last year. We pointed out that the marking of a man practically for life for an offence of this kind was not quite in the order of things according to present-day ideas. The Acting Solicitor General has now agreed to raise the amount to $500; that is an improvement over the provision of last year. It does seem to me, however, that it is for the trader to get a report upon these pedple before he deals with them. To take from a man the right to do business at all in his own name and then place him under a penalty of a year's imprisonment for failure to disclose certain things is, to my mind, like "seething a kid in its mother's milk." However, if my hon. friend raises the amount each year in the same ratio as he has raised it this year, I think we shall soon agree. Last year we were opposed^ to this section and this year the Acting Solicitor General has come round to our view.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I do not know that I have.

Well, he has expressed his view in the amendment, which is supposed to contain the combined wisdom of himself and of the Government in this matter. I am glad to know that he comes round to our view, even if it takes a year for him to do it; as we say in French, "mieux vaut tard que jamais."

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
There is a great deal to be said in favour of the small amount. I can well understand the position of a retail merchant who is approached by a stranger with a request for credit-a man who has come from some other town where he is an undischarged bankrupt. Now, his asking for credit without disclosing the fact 
that he is an undischarged bankrupt is fraudulent concealment, though $50 does seem to be a small amount in respect of which to render a man liable to a year's imprisonment. I thought that $200 would be more appropriate; however, if the committee is content with leaving it at $500, as in the Bill, I shall not raise objection.
Without this clause at all, such a person could be proceeded against under the Criminal Code, could he not?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: There is a general clause to cover that, yes.
That is one of my chief reasons for objecting to the clause.
Does this law do away with all provincial laws respecting bankruptcy? I was not here last year when the matter was under discussion.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Any provincial law heretofore in force which dealt with the question of bankruptcy or insolvency will be superseded by this one.
Unless the Privy Council decides otherwise.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I think my statement is in accordance with the decisions of the Privy Council so far as we have had them.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 19-repeal of section 97:

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Section 97 is a peculiar section. It provides that:
Any person who maliciously institutes or carries on against any person who has not done or suffered any act of bankruptcy proceeding in bankruptcy under this Act shall be guilty of an indictable offence and liable to a fine not exceeding one thousand dollars or to a term not exceeding two years imprisonment, or to both such fine and such Imprisonment.
It was to prevent the institution of bankruptcy proceedings maliciously against any person. We had quite a heated discussion on this clause last year; I think that my hon. friend (Mr. Jacobs) divided the committee upon it. I remember that the then Acting Prime Minister (Sir Thomas White) took quite strong ground in the matter; he contended that the public should be protected against malicious proceedings. There is no such provision in the English Act. The present Bill proposes to strike out that provision, but I leave the matter entirely with the committee.

I must congratulate my hon. friend upon his coming to his senses twelve months after we brought the matter

to his attention. The clause was a foolish one; it was not drafted by a lawyer.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Oh, yes it was,-by an excellent lawyer.

Well, it may have been drafted by a lawyer, but it did not originate in the mind of a lawyer. It originated, I understand, in the minds of the Retail Merchants Association. I can quite understand, therefore, why it should have read as it did. " A shoemaker should never go beyond his last." But what I particularly regretted was that that association should have had sufficient influence with the then Acting Prime Minister to cause this provision to be put in the Act. It was all right enough for discussion outside the House, but solemnly to adopt it in this House as part of a statute was a piece of nonsense. Before this Bill was introduced this year I had introduced a Bill which had for its object the repeal of this clause together with a number of other clauses which have been dealt with by the Government. I shall now have much pleasure in withdrawing my Bill. It was just because I thought the Government had not awakened from their lethargy that I brought in my Bill, and, perhaps, that was the reason the Government brought in theirs. In any event, I am pleased to withdraw mine, and I congratulate the Acting Solicitor General (Mr. Guthrie) on introducing these amendments which, I think, will improve the Act in many respects.
Mr. M'cKENZIE: Do I understand the minister to say that the Bill will be reprinted? And when does this legislation come into force?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: It comes into force on the 1st July by proclamation. The Bill will be reprinted in order that the clauses may appear without amendment. A few changes will be made in the rules, but I think in a few days they will be ready for distribution.
Are they printed?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: They are printed in a separate pamphlet at the present time, and in all probability they and the Bill will be bound together.
Have -any trustees been appointed up to date?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: That matter is in the hands of the Department of the Secretary of State. The Under Secretary of State informed me that a very large list of applications had been received, and I think he said that, the applications of certain men had been approved. I have never seen the list, nor inquired about it, but I understand a satisfactory list has been received.
Is the field open to any one?	-

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
Except a Liberal.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Section agreed to, Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

I thought there was an
understanding that the Bill was to be reprinted. It has gone through third reading and is now ou't of our hands.

speechtext: I notice in the Supplementary Estimates there is an item of $50,000 applied on account of an epidemic of smallpox and other diseases. Is that in addition to .this?

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext: Some time ago, a complaint was filed by the farmers of the municipality of Chateauguay in regard to the drainage on the reserve, and I understood that the department was to send officers there to attend to the drainage if it was found that the Indians were responsible. speechtext: It is a fact that a complaint was received and that officers of the department went down. The report is to the effect that a very considerable sum would 'be required. speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext: With reference to the drainage at Caughnawaga, I gather from the minister's statement that the report of the officers who were sent down there is to the effect that drainage is required and that the department recognize their responsibility for the drainage. It is perhaps a little too late to have the drainage attended to for the spring seeding this year, but the same trouble will arise again this fall and next spring. Does the minister hope to have that drainage attended to during the summer so as to prevent the land in the adjoining municipalities being flooded through neglect of drainage on the Indian reserve?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I did not say that the report fixed responsibility upon the Indian Department, but that it was to the effect that were we to take care of the requirements a large amount of money would be involved. I said that the deputy minister had a note made to consult me on the subject at the earliest possible date. There is no item in the Main Estimates for drainage. As to whether there is an item in the Sup-plementaries I cannot say. Indeed, the subject has not been directly discussed with me. We are constantly in receipt of claims that the Indian Department should do this and that because there is a reserve in the district, but there are not many of these claims that are acceded to. This may be one that we should accede to, but I could not give any statement now as to whether it is such an one or not.

I wish to take this opportunity of publicly thanking the minister and the officials of the department for the work they have done at Caughnawaga. I am interested in a way in the little hospital which was founded down there at Caughnawaga by a pious lady who gave up her little savings for that purpose in order to give some relief to the poor Indians. She bought a building on the reserve, but, unfortunately, according to the laws of this land, in spite of the money she spent she cannot be declared the proprietor of that hospital building because the land belonged to the Indians and the Indians are the wards of the Government. At all events, the property is there and the hospital exists, and an excellent arrangement has been made by the department by which this elderly lady with her companions are giving the poor Indians the hospital service

which one might expect in a civilized community. I understand that the department is well satisfied with the services rendered by these good ladies, who receive no remuneration whatsoever. I would ask the minister to send at the earliest possible moment one of the department's experts who look after these institutions down to Caughnawaga, because there are some repairs needed at that hospital. They will entail an expenditure of about $2,000, not more, and with that expenditure this hospital which has been of such service to the Iroquois of Caughnawaga would be made up-to-date. Of course, the good ladies are doing all this work gratis, and as I said, although the building has been paid for out of their own savings, when they pass out of this life it will revert to the department and the Indians. So by making this small advance of $2,000, to be spent under the direction of the officers of the department, the department will in reality be working for itself and the Indians.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I may say on behalf of the deputy minister that I appreciate the words of the hon. member. Will my hon. friend
send Mr. Cheney down there at the earliest possible moment?
