speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The salaries in that item of $259,006 account for $136,155, rations $37,365, fuel, feed and light $17,536, livestock $15,000.
There is a separate item *for livestock.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That is for driving
horses for the agents. Equipment $9,073, buildings 13,906, miscellaneous $43,471. That makes up the total.
What does miscellaneous cover, anything and everything?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Usually it covers travelling expenses of agents, up-keep of motors, ice, telephone expenses, telegraphing, postage, stationery, etc., in all agencies in these provinces.
What is the Indian population of the three provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It totals 34,348 inclusive of 3,769 in the Northwest Territories. Manitoba has 11,935, Saskatchewan, 9,962 and Alberta, 8,682. The total number of reserves is 218.
Manitoba has the largest number?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

What is the situation
of these Indians? Are they earning any-

thing, or do they depend entirely upon the assistance they get from the Government? I should imagine that they ought now to be in a position to help themselves to a great extent.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They not only help themselves, but they are practically self-sustaining. With the help which the department gives them, not financial hut supervisory, they are almost self-sustaining. The Indians of these provinces are not so far advanced toward maturity of citizenship as, generally speaking, the Indians of the eastern provinces are. They have been in contact with civilization for a less number of years, but they keep gradually improving and those who graduate into citizenship and get away from the reserves and get on their own responsibility very rarely fail. That is a remark of some importance in connection with the legislation that will be before the House later on. The great difficulty is the tendency to keep to the old habits in the reserve. When they get away on their own responsibility-of course they should not be put there too soon-they rapidly, and in most cases certainly, make good citizens. In the three provinces they are virtually selfsustaining, with the supervisory assistance which they get at considerable expense from the department. ,

Have these Indians been
thoroughly Christianized?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Inasmuch as that work is not distinctly ours I am not ashamed to confess that it has not been quite perfect.
It is the Lord's work.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is largely in charge of the missionaries of the various churches, who have succeeded to a substantial extent, and I must say that the whole Indian administration of Canada would be far from the success it is to-day were it not for the co-operation of the evangelical churches. There is no doubt about that. Not only would the expense be much greater to the Dominion, but the character of the work could not be of the same advantage to the Indian if we did not have that co-operation. The work that is being done by the evangelical churches in all the provinces is very considerable indeed and very burdensome to those churches, and to them Canada in that respect is unquestionably under a debt of gratitude.
Does the minister include the Roman Catholic church?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Certainly; there is no church more active in the work than the Roman Catholic church.
How is the work on these reserves apportioned to the Methodists, the Baptists, the Presbyterians, etc.? How do they divide up the poor Indian?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The Anglican, the
Presbyterian, the Methodist and the Roman Catholic are the chief bodies which do this work. They all have their respective spheres, and the policy of the department is to delimit those spheres of activity so as to avoid overlapping and a consequent additional expense. They all agree to that and work along those lines. As a rule they are not situate side by side at some point competing with one another for proselytes.
In that respect they differ from the vihite man.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am speaking of ihe
churches.

The churches in their
treatment of the Indian differ from the white man, civilized, so-called, in the matter of overlapping.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have not experienced any embarrassment from the competition myself. I do not know that there is such a difference.

The hon. member for George Etienne Cartier ()Mr. Jacobs) is evidently looking for the Mosaic dispensation but I do not believe he will find a very strong footing among the Indians. I am glad to say that in the province I come from we have quite a number of Indians. They receive very little support but they are very religious indeed-highly religious. Training in religion was given by the Catholic missionaries who went through the wilds two hundred years ago teaching the Indians, and it is to the credit of the Indians that they have never in the slightest degree departed from the early teaching which they received. It would be a curiosity to see amongst the Indians of the Maritime Provinces anything but a Roman Catholic.

In answer to my hon. friend let me say that I am not looking for a sphere of influence for the Mosaic dispensation as he seems to infer. If I were doing so I would be looking for greater mentality than is shown by the poor Indian.

T would like to ask the minister if there is an amount in the Estimates for building a new school on the

Gordon's Indian reserve in the province of Saskatchewan.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.

If that is the case I feel it my duty to bring to the attention of the minister some correspondence I have had with the principal of that school with respect to the condition of the school and the need for a new building there. In the spring of 1918 I received a letter from the principal of the school asking that I should have this matter brought to the attention of the Government. The war being on, I replied to the effect that I did not think it would be possible that the Government would take it into consideration at that time and I did not feel like asking them to do so1. During the past winter I again received a communication from the principal of the school outlining the need of a new building. The letter reads in part as follows:
Gordon's Indian Boarding School,
Punnichy, Saskatchewan,
February 3, 1920.
Sir,-Permit me to call your attention to the following facts :-
(1)	The main building of this School was erected of prairie stones, about the year 1892, and consisted of a basement divided into kitchen, dining-room, pantry and cellar so called.
The ground floor is subdivided into an office, a sitting room, a girls' wash room, and a room used for a sewing room; also, a boys' playroom, and a wash-room, all of which are too small.
The second floor furnishes two dormitories for girls (large and small girls) and three staffrooms.
Prior to 1914, two years after I was appointed principal, no drainage had been provided, although the building was situated at the foot of a slope, and the water, when it rained soaked into the basement, and undermined the walls, which settled, and made the building so unsafe that heavy iron rods had to be run from one wall to another, opposite to keep them from falling apart.
(2)	In 1913, the department proposed to add a lumber story to the present stone structure, and a concrete addition to the rear, and plans were sent me for approval, but the Indians, on hearing of the project became alarmed, lest the additional weight would cause the collapse of the old building.
In 1914, plans for a new building on a larger scale were prepared, and sent for approval; the proposed new building was to be erected immediately in front of the old one, which was to be utilized for different purposes; tenders were to be advertised for at once, and the new building completed by October of that year.
That was in 1914.
In 191/5 the Government had a frame addition added to the rear of the old structure 40 ft. x 18 fit., the ground floor of which is used' for a class room, and the second floor for a boys'
dormitory. This addition enabled the department to increase the number of pupils from thirty to fifty.
In 1910, the department provided for the building a laundry, a small frame structure, but no reservoir was added, and not even eave-troughing was supplied.
(3)	The condition of the old building, ever suitable for an Indian school, should engage the attention of the Department. The floors are worn out, the basement, so long without drainage (up to 1914), is unsanitary, the window frames are decayed, the roof leaking, the chimneys unsafe; there is no heating system, eleven stoves have to be kept up, there is no water supply, water for laundry, baths and scrubing, having to be drawn from a lake two miles distant, about fifteen barrels a week; water for cooking from a well half a mile distant ; there is no room in building for isolation of a pupil suffering from any infectious or contagious disease, a staff-room having to be given up for that purpose when occasion requires.
During the Flu epidemic in 1918, there were fifty-one pupils lying ill in the dormitories, and there was not one sanitary closet in the building ; a man had to be hired to empty pails and disinfect them., from the boys' dormitory, and the ladies of the staff, in addition to nursing and care of the sick, had to do this work in the girls' dormiitories.
In order to keep the school going, I have expended all that could be spared from farm and W. A. receipts in improving conditions. I have had a frame granary built, .at a cost of $400 ; a storehouse, at a cost of $200, an extension of the 1915 addition connecting it with the main building and thus providing another staff-room, at a cost of $3'00 ; and in general repairs have expended' upwards of $300, some of my small salary from the Diocese having been used from year to year in this way, always looking forward to improved conditions.
It is a shame to deprive the Indian children whom we cannot accommodate of their opportunities, and it is an outrage to expect ladies of education and refinement, who, having devoted themselves to the work, were sent here by the Woman's Auxilary, to continue year after year working under such conditions as I have brought to your notice. As a Canadian, familiar with western life since 1884, and more or less in touch with Indian work, I cannot regard with complacency the fact that such a small matter as the expenditure for an Indian school should prove to be such an insurmountable obstacle to the Government of Canada.
I beg to ask you, sir, for a definite answer, as to whether or not the new building for Gordon's School will be provided this year?
An average of at least eighty children can be maintained as soon as the accommodation is provided; we are constantly refusing applications, and do not feel justified in having the full number authorized by the department, in view of our experience last year during the epidemic.
The new building should include infirmaries for boys and girls, unless the department contemplates utilizing the old building, as the commissioner suggested, for hospital purposes, with provision for a trained nurse.
iSome few weeks ago I placed a question pertaining to this matter on the Order Paper. The question dealing with this particular matter was

Is it the intention of the Government to erect a new school 'building' on Gordon's Indian Reserve, Saskatchewan, this year?
The answer to that question was
Final decision has not been made.
A year ago last winter, during the epidemic of influenza, there were some fifty cases in the school and they did not have a spare room for isolation of cases of this kind. There were three deaths from this disease. iLater on they had an outbreak of typhoid in the school. I have here the report of the Inspector of Schools for the province of Saskatchewan addressed to the Bishop for the district. It reads as follows:
Sir,-Through the courtesy of the principal I inspected the above school, and am pleased to report on the good order and excellent discipline throughout the school generally. The kindly Christian spirit prevailing is very evident, as also the cordial1 relations between the pupils and the staff.
On inspecting the work in the schoolroom I found the pupils well up in the different grades, comparing very favourably with the pupils in the public schools. Miss Elizabeth Atwater, the teacher, is doing excellent work, and I have recommended her to the Department of Education for a Permanent Certicfioate.
As one interested in Indian work I would call the attention of your Lordship to the fact that the buildings and equipment are quite inadequate for the purposes of the school. The school at present is filled to capacity, yet I am credibly informed that the number without any special effort could be increased from fifty to eighty.
That is a point that ought to have some weight with the minister and with the committee. This school building, besides being unsanitary, is wholly inadequate to accommodate nearly all the children who desire to attend. There are other reserves close to the Gordon's reserve without school buildings 'and the children from these reserves would attend this school if there was room to accommodate them. These children are growing up without a chance of getting an education.
This means that many Indian children on the neighbouring reserves are being deprived of the opportunity of a Christian education, thus growing up in ignorance-a menace to the common weal.
The danger of Are In the present building, lighted as it Is by kerosene lamps and heated by stoves and without an adequate water supply is very great. It is providential that no tragedy has so far occurred. The Federal Authorities should be vigorously informed that a new and up-to-date school building is absolutely necessary for the carrying on this important work.
All of wihioh is respectfully submitted.
Tours faithfully,
J. G. McKechnie, Inspector of Schools.
This matter has become one of local interest in that district. The people in the adjacent towns know the condition of this school, know that the principal and staff are giving excellent service, and doing all they can under the circumstances with a building that is not fit for school purposes 'and not large enough to accommodate the children who would otherwise attend it. I think the minister should give the committee some assurance that while provision has not been made in the Estimates, a sum sufficient to provide a new building will be placed in the Supplementary Estimates. An amount was placed in the Estimates in 1914 but the work was never carried out. The war intervened, and nothing has been done up to this time. I hope the minister will be able to give the committee some assurance that the work will be looked after this year.
(Mr. MEIGSHEN:	The school to which
the hon. gentleman (Mr. Johnston), refers, is not the property of the department. It is the property of the Church of England and is conducted by them. The direct obligation of the department is to provide the measure of sustenance per pupil that we provide generally in such oases.
That is done in this ease. It is true that the church is anxious that we should take over the capital proposition and build a new school. I fear the letter the hon. member has read is not a very recent one. As regards the description of the lighting system as being coal oil lamps, I am informed that , the department has replaced that and has installed-
It is so stated in a letter of February 3, 1920.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Since that date the department has installed the Delco electric lighting system in the school at its own expense. It is true that other things are not modern and a new school would be much better, but I am by no means convinced that there are not others in a similar position. It is our intention to have Mr. Graham, the commissioner in the West, visit the school very shortly and report on its present condition. I cannot make any statement as to whether an item can be placed in the Supplementary Estimates this year or not.
Am I to understand that the department will, in no case, build schools on these Indian Reserves?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I did not say that.
I know very well that you did not say so.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The church owns the school. If it were our school the obligation upon us to keep it in repair, or to rebuild it, would be much more immediate and direct than is the case when it is a church school owned by the church. Of course we sometimes do take over a proposition when the church is not able to carry it out, and build a new school which would be our property; but we cannot be held directly responsible for the maintenance of a school which is not our own. Now as to when we may be able to take this school over and reconstruct it I cannot say. I believe an estimate was submitted to the department with that intention at a time when we had far less obligations on our backs than we have at the present time. We want to treat all alike as nearly as possible. We are building one Anglican school, one that was much more necessary, according to the information at our hands, than was this one. We try to distribute these schools amongst the various denominations having regard to the immediate necessity of the case and just as fairly as possible.

With the permission of the committee I desire to place on record a telegram which I received a couple of days ago ficin the Archdeacon of that diocese. It reads as follows.
Regina, Sask., 4th June, 1920.
J. P. Johnston, M.P.,
House of Commons, Ottawa.
The Synod of the diocese of Qu'Appelle in Synod assembled desires to place on record its sense of the serious situation created in our Indian work by the delay of the Government in building Gordon's Indian Boarding School at Punnichy for a period of over six years. In view of other buildings having been built during that period the Synod feels that a great injustice has been done to this diocese and to the Indians. The Synod therefore expresses to the authorities of the department the hope that this matter will receive immediate attention and that the contract will be let and the building erected at once.
Archdeacon Knowles,
Sec'y. of Synod, 1611 Sixteenth Avenue.
New it seems to me that the department must have considered doing something in the direction of taking this property over and looking after it, when it placed an item in the Estimates for 1914 providing for the erection of a new building there.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Just before closing the matter I might suggest to the hon. member that he take the subject up with his leader (Mr. Crerar) who has been urging in rather mandatory tones a most ruthless reduction 208
ir. these Estimates. I think his missionary work might very well be done there as well as with the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), to whom he gives pretty good support, who makes the same demand.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I did not intimate that the leader of the hon. gentleman had' his hands on the purse strings. I only intimated that he is crying out to the Government to out these Estimates down. We cannot cut them down and raise them by the same stroke. The hon. gentleman himself is also pretty strong on economy, but I see that his principles are Changed when the matter is one which affects his own constituency.
My principles are not changed at all. I stand for economy, and I Claim we could easily pare enough off the other Estimates to erect this school building.

Perhaps while this matter is being discussed I might say a word to the committee that would throw some light on this question in direct relation to what is known as the Gordon School as well as many other schools of like character. I happen to have the privilege of being a member of the committee that has been working on matrevised edition

ters of this nature indenominationally for the past ten or fifteen years, and I know something of the situation in connection with the Gordon School as well as many others. What happened, perhaps a decade or two decades ago, was that different denominations went into different sections of the country and erected school buildings rather indiscriminately, the Anglican church, of which I happen to be a member, along with the rest. The result was that we have a number of schools in locations where schools should not be, and there are many locations where schools should be where we have none. It is true that provision was made in the Estimates in 1913 or 1914 for the Gordon School. Provision was made at the same time for other schools within the Anglican communion, and I understand within other communions. But the war intervened and made it necessary for the Government to cut out these buildings. Now, my information is that the department is again beginning to take care of the most emergent cases. At the present time correspondence is passing between the different communions-Homan Catholic, Anglican, Presbyterian and Methodist-with a view to reaching a common view, so to speak, as to jus't the locations where the schools should be placed from one end of this country to the other, and to put that whole comprehensive scheme before the Government so as to get the whole Indian, population into the position that will enable them to get the education they, should have. I sympathize with everything that has been said in the correspondence that has been read by my hon. friend (Mr. Johnston) from the principal of the Gordon School, from the Inspector of Schools, and from the Archdeacon of the Diocese of Qu'Appelle, but I also know that the Missionary Society of the Anglican Church has represented to the department that there are still more urgent cases within their communion, without saying anything with regard to other communions. A situation has arisen, for instance, on the Black-feet reserve that demands immediate attention unless the whole tribe of Indians is going to he wiped out on account of tuberculosis and other ills of this character. The bodies that a\e dealing with these Indian schools- industrial schools, in the main-are endeavouring to push the Government ahead as fast as possible, but they feel that having regard to the conditions with which the country is faced to-day they cannot expect the Indian Department to go ahead very much faster than 
it is going. As the minister has stated, they are erecting one new school which has been recommended by the Missionary Society of the Anglican church and they are erecting others for other denominations and providing additional per capita grants to take care of them. There is no larger question than this before the people of this country to-day, and it will continually get larger. Without doubt, within a short time, Parliament will he called upon to vote more money than it is voting now if the Indian population is taken care of as it should be.
I thought that it would be well to give the committee a general idea of what this school situation is, as I have had the privilege of studying it from the inside, so to speak, in conference and in conjunction with the interdenominational bodies that are endeavouring to carry on this work. Bight here may I say that in many cases the indian Department are erecting the building, providing the per capita grant for the maintenance of the children at the schools, and the missionary bodies of the different communions to which the Indians belong are carrying on the practical work of education. I am sorry that my hon. friend (Mr. Jacobs) is not here at the moment; I heard him make a remark that I feel disposed to resent. Perhaps he said it thoughtlessly, but he remarked that if he was going to undertake the work of proselytizing any particular class of the people he would go to a class with a higher mental capacity than that possessed by the Indians. Well, I suggest to him that he will have to go somewhere else than to Central or Eastern Europe to find that class. The native Indians of this country, given a fair chance, will make just as good citizens as any other men, white or black, that come within our borders.

In this appropriation there is an item of $10,000 to prevent the spread of tuberculosis. I am sure that throughout Canada a great deal of sympathy is felt for the Indians on account of the ravages that tuberculosis and smallpox are making amongst them. I was going to suggest to the minister that this is a possible opportunity of handing over this branch of the work of the Indian Department to the Health Department, unless that has been done already. I do not know that there is any phase of the work of the Health Department that is more important than that of making proper provision for the health of the poor Indians. I understand that frightful ravages are being made amongst them by tuberculosis, and their conditions of life are certainly not such as to preserve them from the ravages of that deadly disease. I should be pleased to know that at the earliest possible moment that that branch of the department was going to be transferred to the Department of Health and that proper steps would be taken to look after these Indians. I am sure that even though we are striking hard for economy now, if more money is wanted for this purpose the people of this country would be willing to spend it.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The Health Department has no power to take over the matter of the health of Indians. That is not included in the Act establishing that department. It was purposely left out of the Act. I did not think, and I do not think yet, that it would be practicable for the Health Department to do that work, because they would require to duplicate the organization away in the remote regions where Indians reserves are, and there would be established a sort of [DOT] divided control and authority over the Indians which would produce confusion and insubordination and other ill effects among the Indians themselves. However, we get every possible assistance from the Health Department. The deputy minister advises me that Dr. Amyot, the Deputy Minister of Health, and his officers have been enthusiastic in their co-operation- with the Indian Department in connection with the recent ravages and health matters generally.

I am not so much concerned, nor are the people of this country, as to which department does this work,
as that it be done. I am not speaking for myself but for a great body of Canadian people.

What is the policy of the department in regard to the employment of medical attendants for the several reserves throughout the country? Is the policy the same in every province? If not, what is the policy in regard to this matter in the province of Ontario? Are the medical men who are employed paid fixed salaries? Who appoints them? Upon whose recommendation are they appointed, and what is the policy generally?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
They are usually,
though not always, paid a fixed salary. It depends upon the circumstances, the amount of work there is to do, and the availability of a man to do it. There may be a man available whom you can get to do the work incidentally, and not a man available whom you can get to do the work on salary. These two factors control. The Civil Service Commission in every case appoints the salaried men.
These medical men?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
Since how long?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Since the Act came into effect. There is no patronage.

The second item under
the head of " General " is " relief to destitute Indians in remote districts, $65,000." There is a similar item for all the provinces where provision is made for the Indians. For Ontario and Quebec I find an item of $42,700 for "relief, medical attendance and medicines," and for Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and Northwest Territories an item of $149,000 for " supplies for destitute." Then there is an item of $11,000 for "relief in Nova Scotia, $10,000 for " relief " in New Brunswick, $13,000 for " relief and seed grain " in Prince Edward Island, and $22,000 for " relief to destitute " in British Columbia. Now I understand that in all the provinces except the Northwest Territories there is a regular organization to take care of these Indians. The remote districts would only be in the Northwest Territories, I presume, where the Indian population, according to the figures that have just been given, is only 3,369. Yet we find the sum of $65,000 allotted for relief to destitute Indians in remote districts. That relief work seems to be covered by item No. 263.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Not exactly. This item is intended to look after the Northwest. Ter-

ritories and also Northern Ontario, Northern Quebec, Northern British Columbia, and the Ungava District of Quebec. There is no item under the provincial headings for these districts. In these remote regions the destitution is often severe and the cost of provisions very high, and it is necessary to vote this amount to meet the expenses. In the northern parts of Ontario and Quebec, particularly Quebec, the Indians have suffered extreme hardships owing to the failure of the fur trade, and distressing tales of suffering and hardship have reached headquarters. It is necessary to make provision for the hunting Indians. This vote applies to the districts where we have no agents.

Lumbering operations
extend pretty far north in Quebec now, and I would think there would be very few Indians who would not be able to take care of themselves, right up to the lake St. John region.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They are away north of there. In the Ungava district the 'Indians are stretched pretty nearly up to the Hudson Straits. I have had a talk with the Rev. Mr. Walton, who has lived among the Indians for many years, and the tales of distress he brings are really excruciating. The difficulty is that the caribou or rein' deer, upon which the Indians live-these are hunting Indians-were either destroyed or driven farther east and south by the great fire about thirty-five years ago. Owing to the virtual extinction of that source of supply, the Indian has not had means to sustain himself, and he has become more and more inclined to get into tents and huts and depend upon assistance from the department and the Hudson's Bay Company, and the like. In that way his health has deteriorated. We are now attempting to establish some reindeer herds up there to give them employment that will keep them outside, and provide them with food at the same time. I only rose to say that the Indians to whom this vote applies are farther north than the hon. gentleman has in mind. I cannot give the exact details as to where each dollar went, but that will be found in the Auditor General's report. The actual expenditure for the year 19171918 was $85,577.35, and for 1918-1919, $65,286.67, or about $20,000 less than the year before.

How do these cases come to the notice of the department, and how are they taken care of?

(Mr. MEIGHEN: Through traders, the Northwest Mounted Police, and the Hudson's Bay Company.

Can the minister tell me what was paid in the last fiscal year to the medical attendant for the Indians in the south part of Middlesex, at Muncey? How much was paid in salary, and how much in extras, if any? If there is more than one attendant, who are they?

I see under the head of "general" an item of $10,000 to prevent the spread of tuberculosis. Would the minister tell me-I was not present earlier in the evening-how this money was spent? Is it paid to physicians who go to the reserves? Are there sanatoria in different parts of the country where the Indians who are supposed to be suffering from tuberculosis are received and treated?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: This money is spent in the providing of hospital treatment for those who can avail themselves of it, and also' in providing methods of sanitation, the destruction of infected houses, and rebuilding to combat the spread of disease. There was spent in 1916-17, $10,792.19; in 1917-18, $10,196.35; and in 1918-19, $13,498. Wherever possible the Indians are taken to hospitals.

Is tuberculosis increasing or decreasing among the Indians, or is it stationary?
!Mr. MEIGHEN: I am afraid 'I cannot give a very encouraging answer to the question. It is the one dread disease of the Indian. We are not convinced that it is increasing, but it is not decreasing.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I shall take into consideration the observations of my hon. friend. There would be an advantage in having the agent at Riviere du Loup.
Mr. McGIBRON (Muskoka).:	What
power has the Indian agent or the medical adviser to order treatment in a case of tuberculosis breaking out among the Indians?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The agent has no final power in himself, but the Superintendent General, under the Act, has power to make an order authorizing the placing of any infected person, or any person who should be treated in a hospital.	,
Mr. McfGIBBON (Muskoka):	What
would the medical attendant have to do in the matter?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He would simply report by wire or letter to the department at Ottawa iand get an order. An hon. member asked for the name of the medical attendant at Munsees, and his salary. His name is Dr. W. H. Woods of Mount Brydges, and he attends the Chippewas, the Munsees, the Oneidas of the Thames Reserve, and also all the pupils of the Munsees Institute. He is allowed a salary of $1,700 per annum, of which ,$250 is chargeable to school fund and $800 to band fund. There is no record here of any additional sums.
How many Indians are there on these reserves?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am informed that
there are about 1,200 or 1,500.

Does the medical attendant
get anything for extra attendance on individual Indians, or is that his full salary?
He gets something extra in the case of epidemics. I have given his regular salary. I have ho record of extra payments; in normal conditions this is all he gets.
Is his salary increased from year to year?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No; it has been stationary for some years. I do not know what it would be under the re-classification.

Is it the
intention of the department to sell the timber on the Indian reserve in Gibson,
and if so what disposal will be made of the money?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
In the case of that reserve, the department has been giving Indians permits to take out timber themselves. It has not been decided to sell the timber yet.
Indian education, $1,064,415.

In our part of the
country we find that the Indian's capacity for education is rather circumscribed. The Indian child is able to read and write pretty well and has a fair knowledge of arithmetic, but the teachers tell me that beyond that, in the field of English grammar, composition, history, etc., it shows an aversion to concentrated study. I should like to know how the Indians in the West get on, and what results are obtained from their educational training.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
As regards the day
schools in the West, I fear there has not been [DOT] any great success. The chief difficulty has been to get the Indian child to attend with sufficient regularity to make progress. The boarding school is the proper system of Indian education for Western Canada. In the boarding school I have never heard of any special class of subjects in which the Indians are deficient or in which, indeed, tney are not the equal of the white children, if they would attend with the .same regularity and give the same attention to their studies. I have discussed the matter very frequently with teachers in those Indian schools and they speak in the highest terms of the capacity of the Indian children as a general rule. But the great trouble is that just as soon as the child gets out his tendency is to revert back to the reserve. Those of his own blood are not earning their living out in the world and he has not his own class with whom he can associate outside; consequently his tendency is to go back to the reserve, and in a short time the value of his education is largely lost. That fact also has a bearing on the question of the wisdom of encouraging and enabling the Indian to the utmost extent possible, consistent with his own fitness, to be enfranchised and be out away from the reserve fighting his way in the world like other people. Undoubtedly, the education will help the Indian children when they come out of the Indian school for they will be equipped, so far as education goes, to make a living.

A question was asked
by the hon. member for Last Mountain (Mr. Johnston) as to the appropriation for a particular school, and the letter which he read showed a pitiful condition of things in that school. Now, the amount we are asked to vote is $1,064,415 for 34,000 people.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speechtext:
The total population of
the Indians?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes,

on the reserves? I had the impression the schools were on the reserves?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It is exactly the same
as last year, and certainly it is none too much; we would like to be able to afford more. There ought to be more Indian board-

ing schools built and we would like to build the one in Last Mountain if we could afford to undertake it with the money in hand, as well as others equally urgent.
Mr. BUREAU!:	How many are there?
Take Manitoba where the population is the largest.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speechtext: Is the school at Qu-Ap-pelle a boarding school?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It is an industrial
school. It really is a boarding school.
Mr. iBELAND: Is not that one of the bes-t Indian schools you have now?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is out of the Qu'Ap-pelle school that the File Hills colony has come. The File Hills colony is undoubtedly a phenomenal success. The number of day schools in the Dominion is 248, boarding schools 58, industrial schools 16, total 322. This is a vote for the maintenance of these schools.
It is not too much.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: And for the construction of such school buildings as are contemplated for next year.

And the maintenance of
the old schools?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The maintenance of
the whole of them.

Is it not possible to comply with the request of the hon. member for Last Mountain (Mr. Johnston) under the conditions existing there? It seems a pitiable state of things if the letter contains the truth.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It was not altogether
right; it was not up to date in some respects.
Out of this amount will there be anj^ money which can be used to improve the condition there?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No.
Mr. B'UREAU:	Is there any other
amount which will be used for that pu -pose?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.

Before passing from the question of the education of the Indians, I would like to make a few remarks in regard to the Indians in the county of Brant. We have there the largest number

of Indians to be found on any one reserve in Canada, or in North America-I think about 4,500. The hon. member for North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) raised a question about them being circumscribed in their education. I have been in very close touch with a good many of the Indians and I think that does not apply to this tribe. The Six Nation Indians are amongst the most intelligent, if not the most intelligent, on the North American continent and they are capable of a very fine education if they have the opportunity. I know that in several instances they have taken very important positions almost immediately after they have passed out of the public schools. I heard of one last week who entered on a commercial course and, just fresh from school, received a salary of $20 per week for her services. 'That goes to show that if the Indian has a fair chance he is capable of very substantial advancement. I would like to know if there is any fund, or whether there can be any fund, provided for those Indian boys and girls, who wish to push on beyond the common school and take a high school course. There are some few in our city who are taking the high school course at the present time. There has been a contention between the city and the county as to who shall pay the fees of these children coming in from the Mohawk institution and from the reserve and completing their course in the high school of the city. The city keeps up the high school and it is customary to charge * country pupils for the education they receive. It appears to me that if the department wishes to advance the education of Indian children there should be a fund provided that might be drawn upon in order that these boys and girls who have got as far as they can in the common school should have an opportunity of prosecuting their studies farther in the high schools of Ontario particularly. I am not sure that any fund of that kind exists; I have not heard of it. But I know that recently there has been quite a sharp controversy in the county of Brant on that very point. I would like the minister to say whether or not there is an opportunity for those who wish to take the higher branches that are taught in the high schools and collegiate institutes, where the parents are not able to pay the fees, and whether the department has a fund out of which it can pay a whole or a part of the expenses of those students while they pursue the higher branches of education. I feel certain that if these facilities were extended and if such a fund were provided, a
very large number of children on the Six Nations Indian Reserve would take advantage of it, and that a large number of them would take a place among the most advanced of the white population. I am sure they have the capacity to do that and we only need to look to what has been accomplished in the last generation for confirmation of my statement. One Indian at least became one of the foremost citizens of Toronto and received a salary of $12,000 a year as head of the Independent Order of Foresters.
Oronhyatekha.

He was a well known Indian, a credit to the country and to the reserve from which he came. I mention that case in order that the committee may realize that there are sons of the soil among our own original population who are capable of the highest education. I certainly think that the department, if they desire to encourage higher education, should make it easy for these scholars who wish to press on from the common schools of the reserve or the country schools which they attend, and to go to collegiate institutes and high schools and that, if necessary, a fund should be provided to help them while they are passing through. I believe in many cases you will find that no inconsiderable number of Indians have made their way in the world by reason of the education they have received. I know several of them from our reserve that have gone to New York, and other great cities of United States, and hold very high positions indeed at very fine remuneration. I feel confident that the Six Nations Indian is capable of higher education to a considerable extent, and if the minister would give us assurances that they would be treated a little more liberally with regard to the fees in these higher branches of education I feel confident that more of them would take advantage of it.
Have they got a vote?

Some of them have the vote. I believe that of the number that went overseas nearly four hundred had the vote,. and that nearly all of them voted at the last election. That is a matter, though, that does not particularly concern myself as they belong to the North Riding of Brant. I am speaking now on behalf of the Indian, and I trust the minister will give that feature to which I have alluded his serious consideration so that those Indians who desire to pursue the higher

branches of education should be induced to do so.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There are quite a number of Indians, particularly of the Six Nations reserve, fwho do desire and do obtain a high school education. With respect to that reserve, the Indian parents for the most part, are quite capable financially of supplying their children with that education, and as to them the department has merely encouraged the attendance of those children at school by awarding scholarships to help them through. But there are others, fewer in number, who are not in the same position, and in those cases the department has always sympathetically received any application for help, and a large number of pupils are being helped by the department in the securing of a high school education at the present time. The ear of the department has been sympathetic to the ambitions of any pupils whose parents are not able to provide them with the fees and the necessary books for the purpose.

I realize that many of these Indians are capable of a very high education, but in view of the conditions in which the finances of the country are to-day I hope the minister will not for one moment think of laying aside tens or hundreds of thousands of dollars for any such purpose. I have brought to the notice of some of the departments instances where the parents of young wrhite men,-young men who went overseas and fought for this country-were poor and were not able to put their sons through the high school; these had to do the best they could to get through. Why then ehould we set aside hundreds of thousands of dollars to give higher education to young Indians when our own white people cannot put themselves through? I realize that many Indians went overseas and fought for the Empire and we ought to treat them just the same as we would any other class of people, but we are not in a financial position to do what has been suggested; and to my mind no hon. member should get up here and advocate that we pay out a lot of unnecessary money for this purpose. I believe in- fair play to every one in the Dominion, but I am also of the opinion that if we iwere to do more to assist our white people we would better serve the interests of our country. There is no doubt whatever that the sons of poor people are just as capable of learning els the sons of the rich; but in many cases they have to do without the education they need because they are not able to put themselves through. I hope the minister will

not for one moment consider laying aside hundreds of thousands of dollars for any such purpose as suggested.
Who is asking for hundreds of thousands of dollars?
Well the hon. member advocated the expenditure of money for this purpose.

If the educational aspect of this matter is disposed of I would like to introduce another, which perhaps more particularly affects the Indian reservations in the West. I have at present in mind the White Bear reservation located on the southern slope of the mountains of Saskatchewan. It is tributary tp a large preserve on which wild game abounds, and I have wondered if the Indian, in a location such as that, is permitted to hunt all the wild gaane that comes there. I believe it is the custom, whether it is the law or not, and I wondered if the Dominion Government permits the Indian to do that, or whether it is a privilege granted by the Provincial Government.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The Indian outside his reserve must comply with any provincial restrictions with respect to hunting or the preservation of game. The Indians have sometimes resisted the imposition of these restrictions by the provinces, but the policy of the department has been to get them to comply. On the reserve itself, I am disposed to think, the Indian is not so restricted, and his aboriginal rights to hunt in that reserve are quite free from any provincial law. I do not want to give that as .a final opinion, but that is my impression.
Government of the Northwest Territories- $7,000.

What is this money
used for?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That is the entire
amount expended on the whole government of the Northwest Territories of Canada, an area I suppose as big as Europe. The Interior Department administers the whole territory for the sum of $7,000, and the minister does not make any extra charge.
What is the population?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: According to the census of 1911 it was 17,196. I doubt if it would he any more than that now. Owing to the extension of the provinces of Quebec and Ontario a deduction would have to be made, but the figures do not include all the Eskimos on the Arctic.

Are we providing for
the government of Eskimos?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
Are we providing them with schools or anything of the kind?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, there is an item of $3,000 for schools included in the $7,000. It only takes $4,000 to govern them outside of the cost of the schools. Last year the appropriation was $8,000, so there is a saving this year of $1,000.
Where is the area embraced in the Northwest Territories? Is it the region between the northern boundaries of Alberta .and Saskatchewan and the Arctic circle?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, north of Alberta, Manitoba and Saskatchewan and south of the Arctic .ocean. The area is 1,242,224 square miles, two-fifths of the whole area of Canada, and a rich territory it is. Negotiations are now proceeding, which will almost certainly eventuate successfully, for the lease for commercial purposes of practically the southern half of Baffin's Land. It is a great mistake to assume that the area of the Northwest Territoriese is wholly -or, indeed, in any substantial degree- barren. The time will undoubtedly come when it will be a prized portion of the Dominion.
Have the Government taken any steps toward finding out whether there is oil in these regions?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The Government, of
course, are not themselves prospecting for oil. The Geological Survey, under the Mines Department, has general charge of the geological investigations carried on throughout the Dominion. The regulations respecting oil throw the opportunity of prospecting and discovering open to every person, and many are availing themselves of the opportunity. In 1913-14 it was generally felt that we were on the eve of very great oil discoveries. There have been none yet of any major importance. T am not sure when these discoveries will be made or whether they will ever be made, but the prospects are indeed bright. I have no doubt that those engaged in the work anticipate that it will not be long before discoveries are made. The Government .are merely laying the scientific basis and in that way enabling these investigations to proceed along sound and sensible lines.
Do you afford any assistance to those who are looking for oil?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No; if they discover the oil they get their own reward. Very large sums of money have been spent in the search, but it has been private capital, not the capital of the Government. I believe that one company has already spent almost a million dollars, so far without success.

The oil resources of the world are nearing exhaustion. Great efforts have been made by the British Empire during the last few years to secure a sufficient supply of oil for the future. I think it would be well if this resource were kept under Government control.
Government of the Tukon Territory-salaries and expenses connected with the administration of the territory, etc., $200,00'0.
What is the total population of the Yukon?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I estimated it a few minutes ago at 4,300; I do not think I am very far out. Anyway, it is between 4,000 and 5,000.
This appears to be a large appropriation for a population of 4,300. Has a like appropriation been made each year for several years past?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Oh, no, the appropriation that has been made yearly for several years past has been far more. In' the last two or three years the appropriation has been very much reduced, somewhat to the indignation, I fear, of the population of the Yukon. I did not feel that the numbers there warranted the expenditure that was being made. It is only a short time since the expenditure was twice the amount we are asking now. Of course, the Yukon is a very expensive territory to administer, owing to its location, its climate and the general configuration of the country. The roads are difficult and expensive to maintain; the whole administration costs much more than that of other portions of the Dominion. It will be seen that even this year there is a decrease in the appropriation of $15,500; the reduction last year over the year before was $190,000. The expenditure in 1910-11- ask the hon. member to note the year-was $303,674.94. The actual expenditure this year will doubtless be less than the $200,000 asked for in this item.
What was the population in 1910?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Practically the same as now; possibly a little more.
Does the Government receive any revenue from that region?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, the Government gets a revenue in royalties; 'I will give my hon. friend the figures in a moment. But the country gets the benefit of a very large production there. The output of the Yukon -I speak from memory-is valued at about $4,000,000 a year, so that it is a territory of some importance. The output per capita is very high.
Mr. MicKiENZIE: Is there .any chance of making this territotry part of the province of British Columbia some day and putting this administration under the machinery of that province?
Mr. MEIGHEN; The subject is not under immediate consideration. I do not know what the attitude of the province of British Columbia would he. The hon. member will remember that, two years ago I think, I put legislation through amending the Yukon Act so as to simplify the local ' machinery of administration. There used to be twelve members of the Local Council and that was cut down to three. Consequently, provision is made for salaries for three instead of salaries for twelve, and the salary of each was, I am pretty sure, reduced. We have simplified the machinery of government and thereby greatly reduced the cost. It seems to me that we would not be gaining much by adding this territory to British Columbia. There would be complications; there is some debt on the province of British Columbia; there is no debt-on the Yukon Territory, and I do not know what the attitude of the people of either British Columbia or the Yukon Territory would be.

I would imagine this
would be an advantage to the Yukon. Every province has its educational and other facilities which it is impossible to have in the Klondike if it is administered as it is now, and all improvements which the people of British Columbia have would, in a measure, be extended to this territory if it were within the province and had representation in the Legislature of British Columbia. In that way, it would he an advantage for the people of the whole Yukon Territory to be attached to a province and subject to governmental administration like any other department of the province.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The revenue is about

I see an item "Grant to
Local Council, $90,000." Is there any possibility of reducing the expenditure through reducing these grants? I may be altogether mistaken, but I see no particular reason why the administration of the Yukon Territory should be sustained by grants from the Federal Government. Each province pays its own expenses and the Yukon Territory, as part of the Dominion of Canada, should be under the same provisions as other parts of the Dominion and should pay its expenses. Why should w7e have to give the Local Council a grant of $90,000 a year?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We give every province in the Dominion a grant each year.

But if we take into consideration the respective populations, there is no comparison between the grants that we give to the people of Quebec and Ontario which 'have populations of from over 2,000,000 each, and the grant that we give to the people of the Yukon Territory.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not know just exactly how they would compare. Of course, we get a revenue -from the Yukon; we do not get a revenue from Quebec or Ontario. From the Yukon we get a revenue of $97,-
000.	That leaves about $100,000 that the treasury itself is at a loss of. The hon. member must remember this, the Yukon is a far distant territory, and the cost of administration there is bound to be much greater than the cost per capita in a more thickly settled part of Canada, where the climate, soil and methods of living are different. I have in my hand the balance sheet of the Yukon Territory, and I may say, if I have erred at all, as Minister of the Interior in the administration of the Yukon, it has not been on the side of prodigality. I have received a good deal of criticism in respect of that administration, but this is the first intimation that I have been in any way too generous as regards the Yukon.
I am not going that far; I just want to get the information.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I may possibly have
erred the other way. The balance sheet shows a loss of $10,439.88. The cost of upkeep of roads, bridges and public works is $62,000; grants to libraries, etc., $13,000; hospitals, charities and public health, $28,000; schools; $41,695. Schools have to be maintained in the Yukon and they are managed by the local council, but they are supported by the governing body, that is to say, the Department of the Interior. Then there are travelling expenses and salaries,

$9,785. Those are local salaries. Then there is Yukon Council, indemnity and travelling expenses, $4,320. If you put against that the $90,000 Dominion grant, and the Dominion grant for roads of $50,000 and all their sources of revenue, they still had a loss of $10,439.88. Notwithstanding that, we are not increasing the grant.
Dominion lands and parks, $4,546,770.
I see part of this item is for Canadian National Parks, $666,000. This is an increase of $100,000. Will the minister please explain?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
This increase is due
practically altogether to the increased cost of labour and material. We administer those National Parks. The Dominion of Canada-not federally speaking-that is, not speaking from the standpoint of the treasury, but the people of the Dominion- derive great advantage from these National Parks, advantage not only in having recreation grounds for the whole Dominion, but in the tourist traffic, the returns per acre being figured by the officers of the department as being more for the rocks and waste lands of our parks than even for our wheat fields. Undoubtedly, speaking from the whole national standpoint, it is good public business to maintain these parks. Of the increase, .$55,000 is due to increased cost of labour. Since the submission to the House of the Estimates of 1920, there has been an increase in the cost of labour in the parks ranging from 12i per cent in the Albert aparks to 25 per cent in the British Columbia parks. The amount due to increased cost of material is $16,500. The Dominion Parks appropriations for the last six years has been as follows:	In 1914-15,
$681,730. It was not much below that for some years previously; in fact, in some years previously to that year it was much more than that. With the outbreak of the war, the appropriation was cut down. In 1915-16, the appropriation amounted to $349,670; 1916-17, $349,670; 1917-18, $300,000; 1918-19, $300,000; 1919-20	$566,000; 1920-21,
$666,000. There is no increase except such as is caused by increases in cost. The amount this year is $15,730 less than the appropriation for 1914-15.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext: Has the minister had suggested to him by his officials the advisability of oiling the roads in the western parks? The tourist traffic is becoming so heavy that at certain seasons of the year the roads become somewhat dusty. I agree with the minister that we have no greater source of wealth than the national parks equipped to take care of tourists, who bring an immense amount of wealth to the country. It occurred to me that instead of sprinkling, the minister might make a permanent job of it by oiling the principal roads in the parks.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Harkin, the head of the Parks Branch, a very competent official indeed, favours that being done. It is only a question of cost. The hon. member will recollect that this year we are engaged in a project of some importance, certainly of some expense, and that is the completion of the Banff-Windermere Road. An agreement was made with the province of British Columbia whereby the Dominion Government took over the completion of that road between the Banff National Park and the provincial road that runs down to the Kootenay and then northeasterly within fifty miles of the limits of the province. The province gave us in turn five miles on either side of the road, quite an extensive territory, which has been added to the national park and which was very essential for the purpose. On account of that expenditure we are not going into any other capital expenditures that we can avoid at the present time. I am informed that we oiled some roads last year, and that we are joroviding for oiling some additional roads this year. The head of the Parks Branch favours the extension of that method just as rapidly as we can do it.

Is the herd of Buffalo
owned by this Government materially increasing?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Very rapidly. We have now about 5,000.

How many were there
formerly?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
There were 700. We
have a herd of very great value indeed. The hon. member may have noted that at the recent fur auction sales in Montreal some buffalo heads and robes and some furs were offered there with very encouraging results. The three buffalo heads that we offered sold for $1,025, $610, and $315 respectively. We sold 38 robes at an average of $76. The total amount realized from the small offerings that we put up at the sale was $4,838. Arrangements have also been made for the disposal of the meat of such buffaloes as we find it the part of wisdom to kill, that is, males that we think are sufficiently far on that they should be killed.

I am very much interested in the details given by my hon. friend.

I think it was a wise suggestion that was made some years ago to re-stock our national parks with Buffalo. A fact which is not generally known, but which I happen to know, is that , the idea of bringing back that herd, which was somewhere in Mexico, originated with a younger brother of the late Premier, Sir Wilfrid Laurier. Sir Wilfrid Laurier was very much interested in that herd. His brother was one of the agents of the Government somewhere in Michigan, and had met the owner of this herd of buffalo, and that is how it came about that Canada purchased it.
Referring to the faT away northern regions of which we were speaking a moment ago, poay I ask whether the Government have accepted the idea which was propounded by Stefansson, the famous Arctic explorer, of utilizing reindeer herds for the supply of meat in Canada? I have noticed by the press, and especially by lectures given by 'Stefansson, that he is very much taken with the idea that the reindeer herds, which are very numerous in the Far North, might be utilized for food in the civilized districts, but I do not know whether this idea has taken root with the department or whether anything has been done in connection with the matter.
There is another matter I wish to bring to the attention of the minister. Some years ago the then Minister of Marine, the late Mr. Prefontaine, and later Hon. Mr. Brodeur, sent an expedition to the northern waters of the Atlantic, and reports were made about some very valuable coal deposits in those northern regions. Has anything been done by the department with a view to exploiting those coal areas? Has any definite information been ascertained about their location, and whether they would be worth developing as a commercial proposition?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Replying to the first inquiry as to the utilization of the northern caribou for food purposes, some months ago, on my recommendation, the Government appointed a commission composed of Dr. Rutherford, as chairman; Mr. McLean, the manager of the Harris Abbatoir; Mr. Harkin, the head of the Parks Branch; and Mr. Stefansson, to investigate and report first of all as to the feasibility of the idea, for which, of course, Mr. Stefansson has been the chief sponsor, and secondly, as to any practical steps that might be taken to that end. The commission has held many sittings and has devoted itself assiduously to its work. I may say that the members of the commission have taken the greatest 
possible interest in it, a much greater interest than they ever anticipated they would take when they undertook the task. They have not made a report as yet. In the meantime some practical ideas in Mr. Stefansson's mind developed, and he felt it his duty to withdraw from the commission. Subsequently, he made application himself for a territory in the North. I may say that before that was done, on the recommendation of the commission, three islands in the northern part of Hudson Bay were reserved and set aside for utilization in this way by the Government later on as it might be advised. Then this application came for the lease of what might be roughly described as the south half of Baffin's Land, or more accurately, all the land in Baffin's Land south of the sixty-eighth parallel, and including a strip ten miles wide along the north shore of Lake Nitilling, in the centre of Baffin's Land, which no white man has yet seen. The application was for a lease of thirty years, renewable, of the grazing rights only, for the purpose of the establishment there of a domesticated reindeer herd brought from Northern Europe or such other place as a herd could be obtained. The lease is not signed, consequently I would not care at the present moment to go further into details. In so far as the Government is concerned the authorization of execution has gone through and we await Mr. Stefansson's return here. I believe he has even succeeded in interesting capital. He has interested capitalists who are not strangers to this country but are just that class who would be most likely to succeed in this venture, those of the experience that would warrant a prediction of success, if such could with confidence be predicted of any. So that very marked progress has indeed been made. Having entered into the arrangement with Mr. Stefansson along the lines of this lease, which is prepared and completed, though not executed, and ratified and commended by the commission to which I referred a few minutes ago, we have made rapid progress, and. it really looks as though a practical step was soon to be taken for the development in Baffin Land of a domesticated reindeer herd such as has been developed in Alaska with really astounding success. .There seems no reason why similar success should not attend the enterprise here. The intention is to enlarge the number of domesticated animals year by year by incorporating a limited percentage of native caribou. Of course, proper provisions are made for the protection of the rights of the Eskimo; all rights of shipment,

etc., are taken care of; and the Government is endeavouring to provide for receiving itself certain numbers of these domesticated animals, mainly with the idea of utilizing them for the assistance of the Eskimo and northern Indians who are now suffering very much indeed through the loss of their hunting preserves in certain portions of Ungava and other parts of Canada.
The hon. member (Mr. Lemieux) referred to certain reported coal deposits in Northern Canada. There undoubtedly have been some discoveries of coal in the islands of the Arctic, but I really do not feel in a position to express an opinion as to whether or not they are commercially valuable at the present time. I do not know that the officers of the department have any opinion on that question at least, not the officers of the department of the Interior.

What are the present
regulations governing the hunting of big game in the parks? Is the policy of the department as regards the next few years one of prohibition?	,

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Absolute prohibition.
Does the department intend that after a certain number of animals have been acquired through the protection afforded it will permit hunting to some degree?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The time may come in the not-too-distant- future when hunting may be permitted by reason of the increase which the prohibition will effect. But for the present the policy of absolute prohibition is being maintained, and there is no intention, in the near future, at any rate, to depart from that policy.
What number of buffalo will satisfy the minister as being sufficient to warrant a certain amount of hunting?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The buffalo are not to be hunted in any case. We do not intend to expose them to the hunter, no matter how numerous they become. We rather intend to utilize any excess which we think might be got rid of by the sale of the robe, the head and the meat. That is the use we intend to make of them; we will not expose them to the hunter.
Only the official hunter.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Neither the official nor the unofficial.

I would call attention to
an item' of $4,000, a grant to the Canadian Forestry Association. I should be the last to ask the minister to indulge in any extravagance, but it seems to me that if there is one association in the country which deserves well of the country and of the Government it is the Canadian Forestry Association. Since its inception some years ago it has called the attention of the public of Canada to the fact that our forest resources throughout the country were very rapidly diminishing and that if we did not within a very short time take some action we would be in the same position as the United States; and not having a weaker neighbour I do not know whether we could use any big stick to pass Underwood resolutions. Anyhow, we would have no more wood.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: So that we could have no stick.

Exactly. Since this association has taken up its work it has, by means of lectures and an exhibition car, instructed the people throughout the length and breadth of the country, both the children and the grown-ups, many of whom were in sad need of instruction in this respect, in the necessity for forest conservation. The association has lecturers who tour the country at considerable expense. It is true that their members are fairly wealthy, but to my mind this is a work which should be materially helped by the Government of Canada, and I am sorry to see such a small sum as $4,000 provided for it. You could easily raise the amount to $10,000 and do $10,000 worth of good to Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The amount is the same as in previous years. I believe that the Forestry Association, speaking generally, does very excellent work, and I enthusiastically believe that the work it is undertaking now in the way of public education in the matter of forest conservation is one of great importance. Possibly, if that work develops, we may consider an increased appropriation next year.

Is the Forest Products
Laboratory included in this?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No, we support that
ourselves. The hon. member must bear in mind that the Forestry Association is made up of men who for the most part have a great deal at stake in forest preservation. It is a fairly large body oif men including some more than fairly well-to-do men. It must also be remembered that the forests are privately owned in. large degree, provincially owned in considerable degree, and federally owned in considerable degree as well. Consequently the obligation is not wholly on the federal Government in this

regard. Indeed, the Federal Government goes to very considerable expense in forest preservation itself. We have felt all along that we were doing our fair share in making this grant to the Association because, while the federal interest undoubtedly is great, the private interest is great as well.

The Government is subsidizing to quite a large degree the Conservation Commission which was created some years ago and which was headed for a number of years by Sir Clifford Sifton. This Commission has interested itself extensively in the preservation of forests and in their preservation particularly against fire. Their findings and recommendations have been adopted, I think, by the Railway Commission and regulations have been issued to the railways. I am not in a position to give the details but I intend at some time when this item is under consideration to supply the House with more information in that regard and especially with reference to the preservation of forests.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext:
There is in this .item a sum of $500,000 for seed grain advances:
Seed Grain Advances-amount required to meet uncollected portion of advances of Seed Grain made in tlie Western Provinces by the Chartered Banks to holders of unpatented Dominion lands under the guarantee of the Dominion Government, also including commission payable to banks for collections, fees to Sec.-Treasurers of Municipalities and officers of the Provincial Departments of Agriculture and clerical assistance, etc., Ja'OO.O'OO.
Does that represent the total grain that was advanced?
