I suppose that was tor last year, I figured that on the basis of the prevailing prices at the time and .at a very conservative estimate there is -seed grain enough to seed at least 166,000 acres. Are we to understand that seed' grain sufficient to .seed 166,000 acres has been supplied and that the purchasers have defaulted in their payments to the banks?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes. The drought in Alberta and .southern Saskatchewan was so extensive and malignant that they were not able to pay. Indeed, the amount of suffering entailed on the farmers of these districts last year is, I think, scarcely apprehended by this House. I went through Alberta and .southern Saskatchewan in August last and the condition of virtual destitution that obtained, in many parts was	distressing. It	was	not a
case of unwillingness to pay; it was a case of no crop at all and a struggle to bring the stock and the family through the winter.

That is the reason the amount is so substantial. This is to pay the banks in respect to the advances made by them and not repaid by the farmers. The amounts advanced were very largely in districts which last year unfortunately were drought-stricken, but the promise this year from all indications now-and indeed the worst of the peril is past-is that the crop will be very prolific. The amount advanced to the banks in 1919 was $632,238.31, and the amount repaid to the banks up to date is $78,026.11, leaving the amount still owing of $554,312.20. That is for last year. We had $575,000 set aside to meet that. It was more than sufficient by about $20,000. For this year there has been advanced: Wheat $387,707.50, oats $228,073.71, barley $15,420. All these articles are at such high prices that it does not take a great many bushels to make up a large amount. The total is $631,201.25. We are asking for $500,000, believing that the excess will be paid. These Estimates were made up some time ago but the weather conditions since have been excellent so that it would look now as if'we would not need this amount.
Is this for seed for the present year?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

I asked some time ago how much was overdue and owing to the Government on account of the advances made on purchases of seed grain tor the use of the Prairie Provinces to the 31st December 1919, and the answer I got was: $1,493,121.11. It would seem that the western provinces are getting into the habit of asking the Government to buy their seed grain. It would appear to men coming from Eastern Canada that the time had almost arrived when the western provinces should be able to finance themselves in so far as seed grain is concerned. I would like to know why we in Eastern Canada are required to advance money for this purpose any longer to wealthy provinces like the Prairie Provinces of to-day. No part of Canada is making money so rapidly as the Prairie Provinces are, and this is getting to be a very old story. Some of the Canadian papers published things that happened 25 years ago. Some days ago I came across an item in the Montreal Gazette:

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext:
.	(The Gazette, Feb. 9, 1895.)
Ottawa.-Mr. Nicholas Flood Davin. M.P., is urging that a grant of seed grain be made to settlers in the Moose Jaw and Regina districts. It is questionable, however, whether the request will be granted, as the impression is

general that the settlers In the Northwest have done very well in this respect in the past, and it is about time to call a halt.
That was twenty-five years ago and the halt has not been called. I would like to know if matters are in such a condition that it is necessary to continue to make advances to western farmers in order to finance their seed grain.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
We simply finance the homesteaders, il disclaimed all responsibility in connection with privately owned lands two years ago when I came into the department first, taking the ground that it was the duty of the province to provide for all necessary cases of seed grain and relief with reference to private lands. But where we have men on homesteads they are our especial responsibility. The lands, in the first place are not taxable by the provinces and on that account it is always assumed that they are the special responsibility of the Federal Government. Now that was not always the case. In 1914 was it not?-yes 1914-there was such widespread distress throughout all that country, on account of the total failure of crop the year before, that the Federal Government assumed the obligation as respects private land and homestead land, and an amount of $12,309,607.36 was advanced in all. There were many at that time who said- in this House and out of it-that the money would never come back, that it was gone; and it was argued then that even if it was gone the amount that could be expected in the way of production would be of greater advantage to the country and be better for all than if the destitution were allowed to continue and consequently there be no crop at all throughout this acreage of Western Canada. Anyway the money was advanced, most of it for seed grain, $7,560,000; but for relief alone, to simply relieve distress, $4,748,000. Now of that sum of $12,309,000 up to a very recent date there had been returned on principal $9,444,391.38 and on interest $889,387.55. The total repaid was $10,333,778. Now that is returned notwithstanding the fact that in those very districts in the last three years there have been what you might call two complete failures and one semi-failure-in the same districts where all this was advanced-consequently there has been very little that could possibly be repaid in those three years. If this year turns out as it now promises there should be a very small balance left after that and, of course, we have security for this money. 'Consequently there cannot be the slightest doubt of the wisdom of the 209
help given in 1914. However, all we are doing at the present time is this: We provide through the banks .for advances to homesteaders to obtain the necessary seed where they cannot get it any other way. I do not think we are supplying any relief at all other than seed grains. The province has to take care of the rest, and they do it with very much the same machinery and by very much the same method as ourselves. We guarantee the banks money but we only guarantee them five per cent to get their bank interest, and they are only allowed to charge seven. They must collect the money themselves. Unless they collect it themselves all they can ask us for is the five per cent, and if we pay it we take over the security and have the same lien that they have.
The Government do not collect it then, they pay it to the banks?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, and that is what this vote is for.

Before the item
carries I would ask the minister if anything has been done with reference to the setting aside of some territory .along the Winnipeg river for a national park; also whether Elk island has been set aside as a game preserve? I would urge the desirability of a park set aside in the province of Manitoba. I do not think we have a park in that great province, and since the boundaries of Manitoba have been extended it would seem particularly desirable that park accommodation should be provided.
M.r MEIGHEN: There has been discussion, and suggestions have been made to the department to -set aside territory along the shores of lake Winnipeg as a national park, but no step has been taken to that end. We have power to do it under the Parks Act, but as yet the idea has not been favourably considered. Elk island has been disposed1 of under a long term lease for summer residence purposes and therefore could not be made a game preserve at the present time.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext:
Reverting to the seed grain question, I quite agree with the minister's statement as to the conditions prevailing in a certain section of the western country, from a point west of Moosejaw and continuing along up. I witnessed those conditions myself. But what I would like now to know from the minister is this: The Government knew of these conditions in September last; was the seed grain purchased



at the initial price established by the board, or did the Government wait until the price had been advanced seventy or eighty cents a bushel and make the purchases this year?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The grain is bought locally, but it is first inspected by the seed commissioner and all orders given can be filled only after such inspection. The bank provides the money. The mam first goes to the Dominion Lands Agent and has his application O.K'd or vised by that agent who knows just what farm he has and takes evidence as to what land is ready for cultivation. From the land agent he goes back to the bank. Then there is seed provided, locally inspected seed, which he can obtain. He gives his security and his note to the bank and goes and gets his seed.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext: I think the minister has misunderstood my question. The minister himself, as the head of the department, acknowledges that in September last he realized the conditions then prevailing and knew that that section of country required seed. What I want to know is, was the seed bought at the prevailing price in September, October or November, or did the Government wait until the last prices that were put in in the month of March?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am not sure that I can answer that question. Perhaps some hon. member is present who would know the facts, but my recollection-I fear I have to depend on newspaper reading for this-is that the seed was provided by the Wheat Board at a price of possibly $2.45 a bushel.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext:
Two dollars and forty-five
cents a bushel at the lake port or in the interior?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think that would be the Port William basis; it was less than that in the interior.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext: Is the minister sure of that?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, I am not sure of it at all. I depend on newspaper reading for that. I do not know whether there is any hon. member of the House present who would be more familiar with the subject than I am. However, it does not pertain to this particular item. In this vote we figured on an average of $2.50.

With regard to another
item-not being on the ministerial side of the House I seem to he among the small items-of $1,000 for the Alpine Club of Canada. Now we have just been told that $4,000 is a great deal to encourage one of ['Mr. Robb.]
our greatest national industries and help us to conserve our forests. If $4,000 was enough for that purpose, it strikes me that $1,000 is altogether too much to help people to attempt to commit suicide on our Canadian Alps. Unless there is another reason for this vote, I do not think we should give the organization in question$l,000,

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
If every investment
this country makes produces the return on $1,000 that the grant to the Alpine Club does we will soon be a very wealthy people. The Alpine Club is a voluntary organization which, corresponding with the Alpine Club in Switzerland, explores the mountains of Canada and induces tourists from all over the world to take an interest in the Canadian Eockies and in exploration generally of an alpine character in the Dominion. We could not get that work done as cheaply in any other way. We could not get the interest taken and the tourists to come unless we had some such voluntary organization as this-except, of course, .at very great expense. This is just the kind of organization 'to encourage, because we get the results with the least possible delay. They make exhibits at the Alpine Congress, *which has lately been held .at Monaco, and are thereby instrumental in exciting interest in the Canadian Eockies among those who gather there and who are devoted to mountain climbing and to exploration.

Is that the best reason
that can be given for the expenditure of $1,000 for advertising? I understand the minister to say that by making this contribution to this particular club we direct the attention of European climbers to the mountains that we have -here in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We get their money.

Yes, but the people who
get the money are the Canadian Pacific Bailway Company and the steamship companies. Why should not these corporations pay for this advertising in order to bring the tourists here?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They spend a lot more than that.

They probably do, but it
seems to me that it is their duty to do it, not the duty of the Government. After all, we are not advertising the scenery of our country. If you will come down to Quebec I will show you good scenery. Give me a couple of thousand dollars and I

will advertise it for Quebec; we will form a club and spend it, if you like-we will do anything like that to please the minister. This club is, I assume, composed of wealthy men; mountain climbing is a sport which requires wealth as well as strength and some foolhardiness. Under the circumstances, I think that this money is badly spent. If the minister will devote this $1,000 to forestry purposes, I shall be satisfied.

There is an item here of
$256,000 for surveys and investigations of water and power resources and for administration of water-powers, etc. I would like some information as to the purposes for which this money is to be spent.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: This is the expenditure of the Dominion Water-powers Branch. There is an increase in this item of $39,000. I would like the committee to note that taken all through there is a decrease of about a million and a half dollars in the amount of this vote. The increase of $39,000 is due principally to the following causes: Increased cost of living and expenses of surveys; considerable additional cost arising from the return of many members to the staff from overseas service whose salaries were not paid while absent; certain new work arising under the .agreements which have been executed pursuant to the Dominion Water-powers Act with the provinces of Ontario, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. Although these provinces own their own water-powers they have sought to obtain the assistance of the Dominion Water-powers Branch in the classification and securing of uniform data with regard to all these water-powers.
How many years ago did they ask for that assistance?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Nova Scotia about four years ago; New Brunswick about a year and a half ago; Prince Edward Island and Ontario about a year ago. Only a few weeks ago I received a letter of appreciation from the premier of New Brunswick with regard to the services rendered by the Dominion Water-powers officials an relation to New Brunswick water-powers. Representatives from Prince Edward Island have rendered like testimony, and I know that the Government of Nova Scotia are of the same opinion. There is no doubt as to the value of the work done and of the services rendered to these provinces. That is the main cause of additional expense in the last two years, .and it has been an expenditure that 2091
has undoubtedly been of great advantage to the country.

I should think that the provinces would know what water-powers they respectively possess. It seems to be taking a long time for the Dominion Government to find out what water-powers there are in Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. Surely the country should to-day be in possession of the facts with regard to the water-powers of each of these provinces. Every year we have an Estimate of this sort; yet it is safe to say that the water-powers are not increasing or decreasing. What are we paying for? If there is no answer to that-

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I did not want to interrupt the hon. member; I was waiting until he had finished.
Has any amount been spent in the Ungava district so far as water-powers are concerned?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
We have not had any request from the government of the province of Quebec to do for that government what we have done for the governments of the other four provinces named. Should we be requested to do so we would be quite prepared to co-operate with that province as we have with the others. Now, it is not a matter of finding out what water-powers there are in a given province. It is a question of getting all the facts about the waterpower and getting them on such a reliable basis that they are of some use to intending investors. It is necessary to get stream-flow data extending over a number of years and over different periods of each year so that any one who seeks to acquire a waterpower with a view to developing it and establishing an industry based thereon will know just What he is getting and what he can depend on and thus avoid the wasting of capital. In many cases-indeed, I have a case in mind at the moment-capital has been invested on supposed data as to stream-flow; the data has subsequently proved to be unreliable, and great waste has consequently been incurred. Capital is getting more and more careful in the matter of investment in water-powers. The value of this material can scarcely be overestimated. Moreover, it is essential that there be uniformity in the method of estimating water-powers and; the various essential factors of water-powers. A uniform system has been devised, a system that was tested out recently in a conference in Great Britain on the subject of the whole water-

powers of the Empire; it was ascertained to be the best used 'anywhere, and it is now being copied in all the countries that were present at that conference. By means of the systems of the federal Water Powers Branch, the provinces are enabled to get their data, not only reliable gatehered, but made to fit into this uniform system, so that a water-power at any point in British 'Columbia may be compared with a waterpower in New Brunswick in every factor that goes to make up the value of a waterpower. That is what has been done, and the results are apparent and are becoming more and more apparent all the time. Applications are coming in for these water-powers, and the water-powers of Canada are to-day actually developed to a greater percentage, I think I may say, having regard to population, than those of perhaps any other country in the world. We have now something over 2,000,000 horse power developed on the water-powers of Canada. I think that is over 10 per cent of the whole developable water-power in what might be described at habitable Canada.

I understand from the remarks of the minister that possibly a report has been made to the department by the engineers who have made investigations and surveys. If such a report has been made, I wonder why it has not been published, so that the public would have the information.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The reports are published. I will give the han. member before ten o'clock to-morrow morning more information as to Canadian waterpowers than he will be able to read in two weeks.
That is going pretty far.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: And absorb.
That is better. The minister, in referring to the Commission of Conservation-

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is the Water Power Branch that has all the material. That has been published somewhat by the Commission of Conservation, but the material has been gathered by the Dominion Water Power Branch.
Who is in charge of that particular branch?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Challies is in
charge; Mr. Johnston is next in order.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext: Are these gentlemen hydraulic engineers?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, they are both hydraulic engineers.

Have these engineers
made a special survey of the St. John river in New Brunswick, and if so, what is the result of their investigation?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Smith is engineer in charge down there, and I would be only too pleased if the hon. member would write to the premiers of each of the Maritime Provinces as to their opinion of Mr. Smith's suitability and capacity for the .work.
I am not discussing that at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He has made a special survey of the water-power of the St. John river. I do not know if it is completed or not; but I have no doubt a considerable amount of information could be abtained at our branch, or perhaps more fully up to date information could be obtained from the New Brunswick Government itself, because Mr. Smith works immediately in cooperation with the Government of New Brunswick.

If this estimate was being presented in the New Brunswick legislature, the remarks of the minister's would apply properly. If I were applying to the Premier of New Brunswick, I could probably get more information than I can from the minister now. But this Estimate is for $256,000 spent by the Dominion Government on surveys of different water-powers in New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island. I ask the minister if his department out of this sum of $256,000, has spent any amount in surveying the St. John river in New Brunswick, and if so, what is the result of that investigation. My question is addressed, not to the Premier of New Brunswick, but to the Minister of the Interior whose Estimates are before Parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
This money is not
spent yet; it is to be spent. ,

Has nothing been spent
in the past?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, but not this sum.

What has been spent in
the past?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Money has been spent, and as I informed the hon. gentleman, some of it has been spent in respect of an investigation into the waterpowers of the St. John river. But the result would be very meagre if it were such that a minister, especially a minister who is not an engineer, could from hi!s place in the House give the result to an hon. member opposite.

It would not be any good at all, if it was of that character. The report is compiled in such shape that a layman can understand it all right. I do not know just how far the investigation has progressed in relation to the waterpowers of the St. John river, but the report is compiled and the hon. member is quite welcome to it. He can obtain it most directly by going to the Waterpowers Branch; and I said as well that it would be available in the offices of the provincial Government of New Brunswick. The hon. member, however, does not need to go there; he can take his choice. The report is available there for any intending investor.
Shall the item carry?

I should like to get an answer before I decide on this item. It may be all right for the minister to make the remarks he has made, but I believe the committee is entitled to find out where and how this money has been spent. When we are told during the last four years Prince Edw.ard Island, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick have been using that money to find out what waterpowers they possess in their respective provinces; we ought to know what they discovered in those provinces and whether that amount of money was spent to some useful purpose.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Does the hon. member want me to tell him how many waterpowers there are on the St. John river, what the best method of development is, what the stream in low water season is, what the best reservoir system is, and so on? Is that the information which he thinks I ought to give to the committee?
If the department has done some work on the St. John river, I should like to know what it has done. If no result has been obtained, why spend money in this way?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There are results. Does the hon. member mean that I should put the report on the Table of the House before this item passes, or does he want me to read over all the report?
If the minister has the information, I have no objection.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Then, we shall be here for a week. What is the hon. member trying to do? He surely does not mean that I should read over the reports of our engineers in regard to the St. John river. Those reports are available for any member of the House. If the hon. member desires
that they be put on the Table, there is no objection to that. Does he expect me to give the committee in detail all this scientific information?
My question is very simple.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, the hon. [DOT] member asks me if this is all for nothing. Certainly, it is not for nothing, far from that; it is for the most useful results.
What are those results?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They are embodied in those reports.
Let the minister give us an idea of what those reports are and what the engineers find.
Shall the item carry.

No. I think the hon. member is very fair. This is a large item. Work has been done in the past, and the hon. member asks the minister what work has been done and What results have been obtained. The minister says that is a difficult thing to do. That may be so, but the minister is surrounded in this Chamber by his officers, and if he cannot go into every particular detail, he can give a summary to the committee. After all the minister, even though he is a minister, has to give information to the House when he wants money. We are not going to vote money without knowing the purpose for which it is intended. What is going to be done, with this money this year? If the minister says that it is for scientific purposes, let us know for what scientific purposes. I think the inquiry by the hon. member (Mr. Parent) is very fair and the minister ought to give us the information. [DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If the hon. member will ask for any detail I will endeavour to get it.
How many water-powers are there on the St. John river, and on what particular ones have the engineers been working?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The two I recall offhand are the Grand Falls site on the St. John river, about 50,000 horse-power, and the Great Falls site about 50,000 horsepower. On the Indian river in Nova Scotia the province of Nova Scotia is expending approximately $1,000,000 in development, based on the data obtained through Mr. Smith and the Water-powers Branch. I do not know just what British Columbia purposes doing, but I do know what the opinion of the Prime Minister is

as to the work. Of course, everybody knew that these two falls were on the St. John river. It is not to find out whether the falls are there that the Water-powers Branch is working. The information they gather is as to the minimum and maximum stream flow over a number of years, the best method of developing that water-power, the 'best utilization to make of it, the best system of reservoirs, so as to make the maximum flow of the high season available in the low season, and all such data as that, best understood by enginers, but which is so prepared, though in very detailed form, that anybody can understand it after study.

I gather from the minister's remarks that now they have all this data concerning the falls on the Indian river in Nova Scotia, and Grand Falls in New Brunswick, which I understand to be the most important water-powers of these two provinces, that he would have no objection to reducing this item this year, as the most important work of the engineers must be over.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The investigations proceed from the more important rivers to the less important rivers. I do not think they are complete even as to the powers on the St. John river. The investigations certainly are not completed as to the other water-powers of New Brunswick, and they are being undertaken for the first time in Ontario. It is only about a year since we made our agreement with Ontario, so that is one extra account this year. The main cause of the increase, of course, is not only this co-operative work with the provinces, but the increased cost of surveys and materials.
What kind of agreement has been entered into between the Dominion Government and the Ontario Government in regard to this matter?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I can lay a copy of the agreement on the Table. It is just the same in substance as the agreement we made with Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. It provides for the supply of a certain number of men, by hours, under the Water-powers Branch, and for equipment. They undertake to provide certain supplies, provisions to the men, and so forth.
How much will be expended in New Brunswick next year?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: About $9,500.
In Nova Scotia?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Also $9,500. Prince Edward Island $1,000, and Ontario $41,000.
That does not amount to $256,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, because we have our own water-powers. It was the hon. member for Quebec who said it was all being spent there; I never said it. We have our own water-powers in Western Canada and in British Columbia. We have no agreement with the province of Quebec, but we are just as ready to make an agreement with them as with any other province. Included in the water-powers of Quebec, of course, are the powers of the St. Lawrence river. There is considerable information on that now, and these powers are being pretty much developed, but there is no question that a very great deal of valuable work could be done in that province.
What surveys of water-powers will be made in New Brunswick next year?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The basic work is the stream measurement, not of any special river, but of all the rivers. That goes on concurrently. The staff is also engaged in gathering other data, first, as regards the major water-powers, and next as regards the minor water-powers.
Under the agreements the minister has referred to do the provinces pay a part of the expense of the surveys and investigations, and if so, what part?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The division is something like this: The Water-powers Branch does the main basic fundamental work in order that it may be done the same in all the provinces, and in order that the information may be related to fixed standards. Then the province does the special detailed work.
Has this department anything to do with the protection of fish where a water-power is being developed on a river?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In Western Canada, where we own the water-powers, when we are making an agreement with the party who develops the power we insist that he provide a fishway, and I have no doubt that the provinces would similarly provide with respect to their water-powers in any agreements made by them.

I am calling this matter to the attention of the minister because all the provinces are not following the same practice. The requirements as to the construction of a dam and fishway are not the same in all the provinces. I would impress on the minister and the department that if

they would draw up plans and specifications which would be distributed to every province, so that we would have uniformity in the building of dams and fishways, they would be rendering a good service to the country at large.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think that is especially the province of the Department of Marine and Fisheries. We comply with t-heir regulations in connection with all our water-powers in Western 'Canada, and I would expect the -provinces would comply with the same regulations, this being a fisheries matter, so there should be uniformity.

I have seen in the papers that it was the intention of the Government to hand back to the western provinces their natural resources. If that is correct, will the water-powers be included in those natural resources?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I cannot say whether
they will or not. It would depend on the final result of negotiations. I have taken the ground that it would be better not to include them, for the reason that the rivers upon which the water-powers appear are interprovincial rivers; and the control of those rivers, as regards the water-powers as well as irrigation, would seem to me to be better within the purview of the federal authorities. It would have been better for Ontario and Quebec had that rule applied. I have heard many authorities say that there would have been much better development of the Ottawa river, for example, had it not been for the divided authority on either side. However, it is not for me to say whether the water-powers would go with the other resources or not. I only express my individual opinion when I say that I think it would have been better for all concerned if this were not the case.
Investigations, triangulations, precise levelling, topographic and field astronomic work, etc., $291,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
There is an increase in the Geodetic Survey Branch. We have 21 men back from overseas, and last year's vote was cut down to such an extent that we could not keep the men in the field. We were paying them salaries but had to bring them in before the season was nearly over because we had not money to supply the equipment to go on; and at the same time we were called upon by other departments to prosecute geodetic surveys, for several of the departments depend upon us in that respect. We have these men back from overseas, and unless there is an increased vote we shall either have to dispense with
them, although their services are required, or else utilize them half of the time and pay them all the time. That is the reason I ask for this increased vote. We desire to use the men all of the time to good advantage.

Does the minister not consider that the work of the different survey departments of the Government might be concentrated and centralized under the Geodetic Survey Branch, as in the United States? In the minister's department there is a Topographic Survey, and there is a Tidal -Survey in the Marine Department, and it seems to me that there may be some duplication of work. Perhaps it might be in the interest of efficiency and economy to have this survey work centralized.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The matter has been
brought to my attention, and I gathered the surveyors together one day and discussed it. I remember that my chief impression was that there had not been nearly so much duplication as I thought there had been. There is, of course, some duplication, and possibly reorganization under a single head would be better, but there are difficulties in that direction. However, I intend to go further into the matter in the coming year.
Expenses connected with the survey and demarcation of International Boundaries, including $1,0-0-0 to J. J. McArthur as International Boundary Commissioner, $45;7-0'0.
What is this money required for and where will it be spent?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The International
Boundary survey has been going on for years and years. It is nearly complete, and that is why we are contracting the expenditure each year. It is reduced this year by nearly $18,000. -
What part of the country is the work being performed in now?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am informed that
this is nearly final; there will not be much next year. I can tell the hon. member where the money is spent. It is for more complete .marking of the boundary line between Alaska and British Columbia in the neighbourhood of Portland canal and the Unuk and Stikine rivers, this territory having been surveyed fourteen years ago, when monuments were placed at irregular intervals. Great mining development has taken place in those districts close to the boundary within the last few years. The mines are near the boundary, and fortunate-

ly for Canada they are on the Canadian side. In my opinion, there will have to be a permanent commission whose duty it will be to maintain these monuments. I do not think ,we can get along without it, and there will have to be a convention between the two countries to provide for the permanent maintenance of the monuments now virtually completed all along the 5,000 odd miles of boundary.
If this -commission is appointed, is it the intention of the Canadian Government to make the -appointments, as regards the Canadian commissioners, without consultation of the Imperial Government?	(

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not know what the practice is, but I should think that whether there would be consultation or not, the selections would virtually be made by the Canadian Government. The boundary commission .is now composed of officials of this Government alone, Mr. McArthur being at the head of it.

I -asked the question because, as the minister has mentioned, a part of the work for which this Estimate is asked will be done in Alaska. I suppose that work is to put into force the conclusions of a famous Alaskan Boundary Commission, the result of whose -investigations was most unsatisfactory to all .Canadians. As the minister knows, on that commission there were two -Canadian commissioners who refused to sign the conclusions arrived -at by the majority. The Canadian commissioners were over-ruled by the American commissioners, with whom the British commissioners joined hands. I infer from the past, therefore, that whenever questions arise as to the determination of boundaries between Canada and the United States the Imperial Parliament has always made appointments. If, in future, the suggestion expressed by the minister to-night were adopted; that is to say, if the commissioners were solely appointed by the Canadian Government, the results might be more satisfactory.
Progress reported.
On motion of Hon. Mr. Meighen the House adjourned at 1 a.m. Wednesday.
Wednesday, June 9, 1920.
